1983-11-11-critics-cool-to-old-vic-s-blo.source_prefix:
Critics cool to Old Vics Blondel

Friday, November 11, 1983

ROBERT CUSHMAN

London ENGLAND -- BY ROBERT CUSHMAN LONDON THERE HAS been unanimous praise from the British press for Ed Mirvish's renovation of the historic Old Vic Theatre. The theatre critic of The Times, after recalling how dowdy the place used to look, says that it is now a superb compromise between Victorian restoration and modern open- plan design." The openness is particularly noticeable in the lobbies, which used to be horribly cramped; though the most spacious design in the world could not have afforded much space to the crowds who turned up for the press night of Mr. Mirvish's first offering.

WILLIAM SHAKESPEARE: A TEXTUAL COMPANION BY STANLEY WELLS AND GARY TAYLOR WITH JOHN JOWETT AND WILLIAM MONTGOMERY Oxford, 1,250 pages, $137.50

The impossible William Shakespeare

WILLIAM SHAKESPEARE: A TEXTUAL COMPANION BY STANLEY WELLS AND GARY TAYLOR WITH JOHN JOWETT AND WILLIAM MONTGOMERY Oxford, 1,250 pages, $137.50

Saturday, July 30, 1988

ROBERT CUSHMAN

REVIEW BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Shakespeare's first editors were actors. Chances are, they were not very good actors. Certainly they fell on hard times and were obliged to support themselves by putting together texts of Shakespeare's plays - the so- called "Bad Quartos" - based on their memories of appearing in them. This meant that their own characters' speeches were reproduced with intermittent fidelity, while everybody else's came out as wild paraphrase.

1988-11-05-children-s-books-treasured-st.source_prefix:
Children's books Treasured stories

Saturday, November 05, 1988

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN They don't all live happily ever after. Most childrens stories, of course, pretend that they do, but there are some bleak exceptions. Darkest of all is Peter Pan In Kensington Gardens, J. M. Barries trial run for his full-length play and novel about the boy who refused to grow up. Peter, having at one week old abandoned his mother for childhood everlasting in a London park, passes up the chance to return to the nest. It will not come again: "There is no second chance, not for most of us. When we reach the window it is Lock-out Time. The iron bars are up for life."

The devourable Bernard Levin

ALL THINGS CONSIDERED BY BERNARD LEVIN Random House, 305 pages, $29.95

Saturday, July 01, 1989

ROBERT CUSHMAN

REVIEW BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Here is a collection - the fifth - of articles written for the Times (of London) by Bernard Levin in his role as Personality Columnist. Levin is the most celebrated columnist - maybe the most celebrated journalist - in the British press, and quite deservedly so. He is opinionated, unquenchable and writes elegant English, which seems colloquial even when it isn't. (Nobody could talk that well that fast, though in his TV appearances Levin often gives the impression that he might; oh yes, he is also very fond of parentheses and has seduced many into the erroneous belief that they can get away with it as well as he does.) His long, cascading sentences appear to pour on to the page of their own volition, though they must really be the result of immense and painful effort. At least I hope they are.

1989-12-27-beckett-was-a-born-playwright.source_prefix:
Beckett was a born playwright First time out, he produced a masterpiece

Wednesday, December 27, 1989

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Not all authors come to resemble their work, but Samuel Beckett , living on rice and giving no interviews, nearly brought it off. He approached the end of his life as ascetic and unreachable as one of his own plays. Only death itself - last Friday in Paris - has by a typically black Beckettian paradox, spoiled the likeness, imposing a finality that the work itself could never achieve. Beckett's characters court insensibility but never achieve it. He rages, not against the dying of the light, but against its stubborn refusal to go out altogether. He liked low-key lighting effects, but he steered clear of blackouts.

Tuesday, February 27, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail The Music of Andrew Lloyd Webber in Concert, now at Pantages Theatre in Toronto, is slick and sleek. ALL MY BEST FRIENDS BY GEORGE BURNS with David Fisher Putnam, 320 pages, $23.50 REVIEW BY ROBERT CUSHMAN A book of anecdotes, like a dictionary of quotations, is not something to be read. It is to be consulted, dipped into, rifled. A browsers delight, it is guaranteed to put a reviewer in a foul temper. He has to plow through it, thinking about all the real books in which anecdotes have been welcome diversions from the serious business of narrative and analysis. 1990-05-18-sammy-davis-jr-s-early-career.source_prefix:
Sammy Davis Jr.'s early career will be remembered with affection A black performer who succeeded on white terms

Friday, May 18, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail FOR THE first 30 years or so of his career - and remember he started right out of the cradle - Sammy Davis Jr. was strictly a North American phenomenon. Davis, who died Wednesday, was a Broadway star in 1956 in Mr. Wonderful, but the show, though a hit, was ephemeral, best remembered for a hit recording of its title song by Peggy Lee. Over the years, she probably did better out of it than he did. Anyway the show was essentially a blow-up of Davis's night club act, and American club acts have never really been big anywhere outside America. The informed bought his Decca record albums, but to most people he was another U.S. singer, covering the same standard repertoire as everybody else. Some said he did impressions.

ROBERT CUSHMAN

George Bernard Shaw, who had little time for the plays of his honored colleague Arthur Wing Pinero, made an exception of Trelawny of the 'Wells'. Pinero the problem playwright, the Pinero of The Second Mrs. Tanqueray, was in Shaw's view a fake, writing reactionary melodramas and trying to pass them off as challenging pictures of modern life. Pinero, thought Shaw, derived his views of modern life from the work of other playwrights as blinkered as himself. But Trelawny is a period piece - written in 1897, set some 35 years earlier - and Shaw was happy to applaud and endorse its nostalgia.

Thursday, May 31, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Music by Cole Porter Directed by Jerry Zaks Starring Mitzi Gaynor At O'Keefe Centre, Toronto Time-tripping on a musical luxury liner BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail ANYTHING Goes, which opened at Toronto's OKeefe Centre on Tuesday, is the quintessential thirties musical. The Cole Porter score, studded with standards, has a lot to do with this, but the shows main attraction may be its setting. It mostly happens on a luxury liner making the transatlantic run. Something about the holiday mode makes the transition from speech to song seem very natural. Besides, Art Deco nautical can be a very attractive style.

1990-07-05-theatre-review-oklahoma.source_prefix:
THEATRE REVIEW OKLAHOMA!

Thursday, July 05, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Written by Richard Rodgers and Oscar Hammerstein Directed by John Davidson Starring John Davidson and Kim Crosby The latest version of Oklahoma! to hit Toronto should introduce some emotional delicacy in its treatment of characters Makeshift revival needs reworking ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail IT has often been pointed out that an old-fashioned show about Oklahoma (you think Oklahoma! is an old-fashioned show? You don't know from old- fashioned) would have started with that song. Wise after the event, we can all see that it would not have had a tenth of the impact that it has at the musical's climax. This is not just because of the architectural advantage of a slow build. It is because, at the beginning of the show there is no Oklahoma, so the song would make no sense: not that that would deter some producers, then or now. When the show starts the characters are living in an unnamed area of the American West (I believe it was called Indian Territory but the show ain't lettin' on); when it ends, statehood is looming. A mere three weeks have elapsed, but that of course is an eternity in politics.

Thursday, July 19, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Written by Andrew Lloyd Webber and Richard Stilgoe Directed by Arlene Phillips At O'Keefe Centre, Toronto The trouble with Starlight Express is that this musical on wheels is, at times, not spectacular enough Exciting, sometimes beautiful, but not always on the right track ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail STARLIGHT Express is one of those shows that nobody likes except the public. It is everlasting in London, ran respectably in New York, and is doing well on the road, if that is the right expression for a show ostensibly about the lives and loves of a set of trains. But critics everywhere have despised it, and the O'Keefe's pre-publicity material was confined to a single word, repeated over and over. The word was "spectacular" and all the critics had used it because they had to. It isn't a value judgment; it's a statement of fact.

Thursday, August 09, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

By Andrew Lloyd Webber and Tim Rice Directed by Tony Stevens Starring Stephen Lehew At O'Keefe Centre Jesus Christ Superstar is an up-to-date Sunday school treat with an impressive score and lyrics that are fresh and intelligent The Passion story as rock oratorio BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail THIS is the way it goes. A lot of street-life is happening in old Jerusalem, a territory with a hitherto unsuspected incidence of dry ice and late sixties tribal bopping. A token military presence, composed of young men in tunics and gleaming ironmongery, polices the quarter in the desultory fashion referred to in the training manuals as crossing from stage right to stage left and exiting; but as soon as this manoeuvre has been accomplished the locals return to their customary avocations. The righteous among them go looking for prostitutes to insult; the free- thinkers spring to the ladies defence; and there is a violent outbreak of Choreography. Then a long-haired young man in off-white Biblical togs appears atop the flight of steps that is the places principal architectural feature, and everything and everybody goes very quiet.

1990-08-21-appreciation-the-extraordinar.source_prefix:
APPRECIATION"The extraordinary voice crooned, throbbed, stomped, shouted. It could soothe and it could lament Pearl Bailey never lost her rhythm or her humor

Tuesday, August 21, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail AN agency report on Pearl Bailey, who died Friday at age 72, announced that Pearlie Mae was best-known for her rendition of Hello Dolly! This must have been news to many of her fans. Pearl - she liked to speak of herself like that in the third person - did indeed play Dolly during the original Broadway run; she was something like eighth in line for the role and represented a desperate attempt by producer David Merrick to revive interest in his long-running meal-ticket by turning it into a black musical. Desperate and yet highly successful: Pearl, uniquely among take-over artists, was permitted to record a new cast album on the score and her singing of the title song, on stage or on record, probably raised the regulation number of goose-bumps. But identified with it? Oh, honey.

1990-09-28-the-new-season-performing-art.source_prefix:
THE NEW SEASON PERFORMING ARTS THE SON KING David Mirvishs theatre empire, stretching from Toronto across the continent and to London, is based on the principle of talk softly and carry a big hit

Friday, September 28, 1990

ROBERT CUSHMAN

By ROBERT CUSHMAN There is a theatrical producer in New York of whom it has been said thateverybody hates him at first sight, because it saves time. David Mirvish has theopposite problem. Everybody likes this gentle, soft-spoken man as soon as theymeet him; I have yet to encounter anyone who has had cause to change thisopinion. Nor does it help his credibility as Canada's major theatrical powerfigure that as his hairline recedes he gets to look increasingly like his evenquieter father the self-made, self-satirizing tycoon, Honest Ed. Still, there must be iron in there somewhere as well as a lot of disposableincome. Both will be needed this fall, as, after more than a year of housing thehit musical Les Miserables, Mirvish and his venue, The Royal Alexandra Theatre,have returned to limited runs and subscription audiences. Meanwhile the worldaround them has, at least superficially, changed. Toronto now has a commercial theatre sector.

THEATRE REVIEW A GAME OF INCHES

Saturday, March 16, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

WRITTEN BY AND STARRING LINDA GRIFFITHS Directed by Sandra Balcovske At Theatre Passe Muraille Mainspace, in Toronto In her latest solo turn, actress and writer Linda Griffiths presents a concoction that's too elaborate to be a comedy and too sketchy to cut it as a play A Game of Inches comes up short BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail IHAVE only seen one previous Linda Griffiths show, the embarrassingly amateurish Maggie and Pierre. I know it's considered a landmark in Canadian theatre, but so much the worse for Canadian theatre. I recall a smug endless monologue that was tickled pink by its own daring at lampooning the First Couple, and laid itself in the aisles at the audacity of having both of them done by the same actor. Since that actor's sole idea of characterization was to portray everyone as Barbra Streisand joke-Jewish, jabbing nasally at anything that resembled a comic point, the notion palled rather quickly.

Backstage with the music men INVENTING CHAMPAGNE:The Worlds of Lerner and Loewe ALL HIS JAZZ: The Life and Death of Bob Fosse

BY MARTIN GOTTFRIED Bantam, 483 pages, $29.95

Saturday, March 23, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

REVIEW BY ROBERT CUSHMAN "THE writing of a book begins long before the writing of a book begins," says Martin Gottfried at the beginning of All His Jazz, unbearably arch before we have even got started on the acknowledgements. But he pulls himself together and offers a riveting account of a life that might have been lived for the benefit of a biographer. Bob Fosse began his career at age 10 as a child hoofer, calling himself Bobby Ritz. At an impressionable age he was exposed to Depression burlesque houses and strippers' dressing-rooms. Life was a cabaret, old chum, and a seedy one. Gottfried makes much - maybe too much - of the unfulfilled performer striving to assert himself in the feted choreographer, but history does keep playing into his hands. Back in 1955, choreographing Damn Yankees, Fosse worked out an aborted routine for a compere-figure in a gorilla suit. In 1972 Fosse was able to take over the gorilla in Cabaret and embrace it like an old friend.

1991-05-31-theatre-review-the-10-000-yea.source_prefix:
THEATRE REVIEW THE 10,000 YEAR-OLD WOMAN

Friday, May 31, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN AND PERFORMED BY CHERYL CASHMAN At the Theatre Centre, Toronto Cheryl Cashman's one-woman show has half a dozen clowns, one gifted and ebullient comic sketch, and plenty of self-indulgence Sincerity is no excuse for embarrassing the audience BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto ACTUALLY, Cheryl Cashman confides at the beginning of her one-woman show, she isn't 10,000 years old at all. She's only 580 but the management bumped her age up so that they might more easily take our money. (This isn't quite as funny as the show gets, but for a long time it seems uncomfortably likely that it will be.) In terms of arithmetic, I suppose Cashman has a right to detain us five times as long as Mel Brooks's 2,000-year-old stripling, but I question her tact in doing so. Besides, Brooks had a first-rate foil in Carl Reiner, while Cashman has only half a dozen painfully grimacing red-nosed acolytes who minister to her needs when she is on stage and move things aimlessly about during the few moments when she isn't.

THEATRE REVIEW THE WILL ROGERS FOLLIES The American satirist said his life story would never work as a Ziegfeld spectacular, but this award-winning Broadway musical takes the plunge, synchronized high-kicks and all An act of folly? Will was right, as usual

Friday, July 12, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

New York NY -- WRITTEN BY PETER STONE, BETTY COMDEN, ADOLPH GREEN and CY COLEMAN Directed and choreographed by Tommy Tune Starring Keith Carradine and Dee Hoty At the Palace Theatre, New York BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail New York IENTERED the theatre knowing little about Will Rogers, but well disposed toward him and mildly curious, and I left in much the same state. Rogers was a homespun American satirist who in the early decades of the century told the people the truths they wanted to hear. He wrote newspaper columns and he appeared on the stage, notably as a continuing star of The Ziegfeld Follies, providing interludes of comic sanity while all around him were getting on with the job of Glorifying The American Girl. The Will Rogers Follies, this years Tony Award-winning musical on Broadway, presents Rogers' own life story in the terms of a Ziegfeld spectacular.

1991-07-13-nat-king-cole-the-smooth-old-.source_prefix:
BY LESLIE GOURSE McClelland & Stewart, 309 pages, $29.95

Nat King Cole, the smooth old soul UNFORGETTABLE: The Life and Mystique of Nat King Cole

BY LESLIE GOURSE McClelland & Stewart, 309 pages, $29.95

Saturday, July 13, 1991

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Review by ROBERT CUSHMAN LESLIE Gourse starts her biography with an "Overview" that commends Nat Cole's "subtle swing" as a pianist, of which his singing style was initially just an extension. Of his ballad singing she remarks, justly and evocatively, "there was a humming quality to his sound that suggested the murmur of a bee flitting around a rose garden," adding that listeners were "touched by the kindness, tenderness and patience in his voice," while his friends and entourage found the same qualities in him as a man. She alludes to the "frightening racial clash in Alabama" when white racists jumped the stage and pummelled him to the ground. Gourse also points to the crucial influence on his career of his second wife Maria, "an unabashed snob" but "renowned for her shrewdness . . . and for her stylishness and taste." She was his unofficial manager, though his official one, Carlos Gastel, was important too; he "had a magic touch."

Friday, May 29, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- WRITTEN BY MICHAEL STEWART, CHARLES STROUSE AND LEE ADAMS Directed by Gene Saks Starring Tommy Tune At OKeefe Centre Rating: Back in 1960, Bye Bye Birdie had a lot going for it, but time and a less than rigorous revival have stolen some of its charm Musical feeling its age BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto HEY says Tommy Tune, favouring the audience with a winning smile that must have been honed by a year of touring, "its 1959." He was responding to a barrage of hisses, occasioned when the guy he plays, a turning worm, starts screaming at his girlfriend that a woman's role is to obey. The barracking was as idiotic as such displays usually are. For one thing, the character at this point is plainly seen to be ridiculous, and, for another, the show is full of sexist assumptions which the same house had swallowed with gurgles of enjoyment. Subtlety was wasted on them; so, apparently, was cartoon blatancy. Tune's reminder that the musical - first seen in 1960 - is a period piece, was apposite and charming. It also raised a lot of questions.

1992-06-06-finally-a-confident-declarati.source_prefix:
BY RUSSELL FRASER

Finally, a confident declaration: This was a man SHAKESPEARE: The Later Year

BY RUSSELL FRASER

Saturday, June 06, 1992

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Columbia University Press, 380 pages, Review by ROBERT CUSHMAN THIS is a fine, unfashionable book, the second half of a two-part life and works of Shakespeare. Actually, it takes in most of the Works. Russell Fraser's Young Shakespeare got his man to London, and tracked his beginnings as actor, playwright and poet. Plague had closed the theatres, and driven our hero to narrative verse. (London, says Fraser, "was a pesthouse.") Then, in 1594, the playhouse had re-opened and Shakespeare, 30 years old, supplies them with Romeo and Juliet and A Midsummer Night's Dream: a tragedy and a comedy on identical themes.

The danger part is that the West End of London long ago decided that its favourite son, the boy-genius who persuades them that nothing has changed and supper is still being served at the Savoy Grill after the show, wrote only four plays worth bothering with: Hay Fever, Private Lives, Blithe Spirit and Present Laughter. Smith and Karen Skidmore At the Shaw Festival, Royal George Theatre, Rating: A big show in its own day, Gentlemen Prefer Blondes is an inconsequential one in ours; and the Shaw Festival's miniature musical revivals are instantly disarming affairs that never pretend to offer us the greatest show on earth Playing fast and Loos BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Niagara-on-the-Lake SUSAN Cox has directed Gentlemen Prefer Blondes, quite niftily, as though it were a 1920s musical. In a way, it is. It is set in that decade and based on one of its classic texts: Anita Loos's study of the theory and practice of gold-digging, the beddable in full pursuit of the bankable. But Loos did not turn her novel into a show until 1949, by which time musicals were standing heavier in the scales. This one spends its first half on a transatlantic liner and its second in Paris, both locations being theatrical shorthand for frothy hedonism. Even so, it lacks the dizzy salacity of its forebears, and its music, written in the aftermath of swing, is beefier. THEATRE REVIEW THE SILVER KING

Tuesday, June 01, 1993

Niagara-on-the-Lake ONT -- WRITTEN BY HENRY ARTHUR JONES Directed by Christopher Newton Starring Stuart Hughes, Neil Barclay, Sharry Flett, Barry MacGregor, Jack Medley and Robert Benson At the Shaw Festival, Festival Theatre Rating: The Shaw Festival's The Silver King is a big, fat, teeming melodrama; and it does seem at times to hold the whole of late Victorian England in its hands. This, though, is more a matter of breadth of canvas than depth of theme Facing a Dickens of a dilemma BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Niagara-on-the-Lake THEY applaud easily at the Shaw Festival, and they erupted when the lights went up to reveal scaffolding, three tiers no less, with lots of actors standing on it. The lights then went up a little more, and we beheld machinery. A massive wheel was there, and it turned, and somebody was crushed beneath it. It recalled the Hal Prince production of Sweeney Todd, and it too seemed to be signifying the fate of man in a newly industrialized society, and to be impressive, and somewhat tangential to the piece in hand.

Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont. -- BY BERNARD SHAW Directed by Christopher Newton Starring Seana McKenna, Jim Mezon and Duncan Ollerenshaw At the Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake Rating: The Candida conundrum In this naturalistic play, in which nothing really happens, there is little space for Shaw the intellectual comedian or Shaw the crazy clown ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Niagara-on-the-Lake, Ont. OF all Shaw's plays, Candida is the least like a public meeting. That sounds like a compliment but isn't. Generally the fun in Shaw comes from seeing ideas hurled through the air from one player to another, and returned at unexpected angles. Shaw the intellectual comedian is entertaining in himself; his doppelganger, the crazy clown, is even better value. The partners are inseparable, and they bring out the best in one another.

He presents the young Napoleon, billeted at a wayside inn while campaigning in Italy and on the verge of decisive military success. Like other Shavian powerhouses, he talks a good game and prides himself on his freedom fron cant and illusion. Also like them, he is outmanoeuvred by a woman,one who acts instinctively on the principles - or lack of them - that he has had to work out intellectually.

Monday, August 16, 1993

Niagara-on-the-Lake ONT -- WRITTEN BY HARLEY GRANVILLE BARKER Directed by Neil Munro Starring Ann Baggley, Seana McKenna, Jim Mezon and Christopher Newton At the Court House Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake Rating: The Marrying of Ann Leete is so precisley styled - as opposed to stylized - that it presents great challenges to its audience and its interpreters. Haunting play never quite comes into the light BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Niagara-on-the-Lake THIS is a fascinating play that begins in darkness and never quite comes into the light. It starts shortly before sunrise in an English country garden. On a bet, an aristocratic house-guest surprises and kisses the daughter of the house. Whether this is a joke, a serious affront, or a sign of actual feeling, nobody seems quite sure, least of all perhaps the assailant himself. Halfway through the play he is engaged to the girl, though not before he has fought a duel with her father. At the final curtain the young lady, Ann Leete, is indeed married: to her father's gardener.

BY JOAN PEYSER Simon and Schuster, 319 pages, $33.95

Saturday, September 11, 1993

ROBERT CUSHMAN

GERSHWIN REMEMBERED BY EDWARD JABLONSKI Amadeus Press, 181 pages, $17.95 Review by ROBERT CUSHMAN LOOK here upon this picture and on this. Joan Peyser directs our attention to two portraits of George Gershwin. One is a Hirschfeld drawing of a composer smart and self-confident, chin and cigar rampant, addressing the piano with one set of fingers elegantly curled and the other aggressively outstretched. The second picture, painted by Gershwin himself is, says the biographer, "melancholy, thoughtful." The world is still deceived with ornament, and it has accepted the picture of an extrovert Gershwin and ignored the pain within.

1995-01-07-theatre-review-the-monument.source_prefix:
THEATRE REVIEW THE MONUMENT

Saturday, January 07, 1995

ROBERT CUSHMAN

WRITTEN BY COLLEEN WAGNER Directed by Richard Rose Starring Rosemary Dunsmore and Tom Barnett At the Canadian Stage Co. Berkeley Street Rating: Treating the horror of war and violence against women as synonymous robs The Monument of its potential power Compelling play not very interesting BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to the Globe and Mail WHEN the lights go up, not that they go up very far, it looks like a scene from a Shakespeare history, brutalist style. A sombrely-clad man harangues us in the gloom from what might be a throne. Slowly we discern that it's actually an electric chair, and that he is strapped to it; the pointy thing on top of his head is not some kind of exotic crown. In the moments before execution he is making confession, though he does not seem very penitent. He is a contemporary soldier recalling the 13 women he has raped and then killed. There is one who especially attracted him and of whose fate he leaves us uncertain. He also speaks of the pressure from his peers that set him off on his career as a war criminal, of his increasing sexual difficulties, and of his own still-virgin girlfriend. What he really regrets, though, is having been caught. It is, as you may well imagine, a powerful speech.

The most extraordinary thing about John Guares play is its narrative, a tall story that grabs the mind and the attention, and radiates in all sorts of directions. Guare - the most promising playwright in the U.S. for an uncomfortable number of years, and also author of the wonderful screenplay for Atlantic City -seized on a newspaper report that had lodged in his mind for years and turned it, in 1991, into his own masterpiece: the best American play since David Mamet's Glengarry Glen Ross (1984). BOOK REVIEW CATS OF ANY COLOR: Jazz Black and White

By Gene Lees Oxford University Press, 246 pages, $34.95

Friday, February 24, 1995

Robert Cushman

Essays that explore race and riffs Reviewed by Robert Cushman IN a feature on racism in the current issue of Jazz Times, Gene Lees is quoted as saying, "If I was a black, I would hate white people, no question in my mind about that." Lees himself is a Canadian who grew up during the Second World War with a pantheon of black American heroes. ("Fifty years ago," he recalls, "it appeared that Canadians had never accomplished anything.") He has spent his adult life in the United States writing about and around jazz. The essays that make up this book provide plenty of grim evidence as to why blacks might hate whites, but are also full of heartening testimony from those who refuse to.

Based on The Bacchae by Euripides Directed by Tadashi Suzuki Starring the Suzuki Company of Toga At Harbourfront Centre in Toronto until Thursday Rating: Drearily predictable world-view mangles Euripides play Reviewed by Robert Cushman I HAD some trouble understanding this Japanese adaptation of The Bacchae, and not just because I don't speak Japanese. Euripides's tragedy, perhaps the starkest ever written, stages the conflict between Dionysus, god of wine and the raging unconscious, and Pentheus, the young and uptight King of Thebes. Dionysus's cult has invaded Thebes, and Pentheus wants to stamp it out. He imprisons its prophet: actually the god himself in disguise. The prophet escapes. He then persuades Pentheus to dress in drag to spy on the female Dionysiacs cavorting in the hills. The women discover and dismember him. Their leader is Pentheus's own mother.

Written and performed by Abel and Gordon At the Tarragon Theatre until October 8 Rating: -1/2 The Escape suffocated by winsomeness Reviewed by Robert Cushman ABEL and Gordon are very good at what they do. Dominique Abel is a sweet-faced Belgian harlequin who, when he perches on imaginary ledges 13 imaginary storeys up, can make you share his vertigo. He can pull the oldest trick in the book of mime - feeling his way along an invisible wall and convincing you it's solid - and render it new. Fiona Gordon, who has the absentmindedly sultry air of an elongated Carol Burnett, boasts a body that bends in all the recognized places plus a few on which the patent may still be pending. She is superb at jumping into bed. That may not sound like much, but her bed is fixed at a steep diagonal to the floor and is some five feet tall at its highest point.

Fiona Gordon, who has the absentmindedly sultry air of an elongated Carol Burnett, boasts a body that bends in all the recognized places plus a few on which the patent may still be pending. She is superb at jumping into bed. That may not sound like much, but her bed is fixed at a steep diagonal to the floor and is some five feet tall at its highest point.

Wherever you look, there's Jane The trend, nay, the bandwagon, for Jane Austen may exist for the moment, but the author's inconsiderately small output is going to make it a short-lived one.

Saturday, January 20, 1996

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto I KEEP reading that the rash of Jane Austen adaptations on film and television is due to a nostalgia for pretty manners and pretty clothes, or that it's a backlash against permissiveness, or that it heralds a renewed appetite for long words and complex sentences. Subtler analysts point to the concern in the novels with money, and with what it can buy in the way of sex and security, and compare this to our current economic pressures. Everybody feels short of cash. It is a comfort to watch other people in the same predicament, especially when they spare our susceptibilities by being in no visible danger of starvation.

BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail COLOUR-BLIND casting is a fine idea, but it has occasioned more hypocrisy and muddled thinking than any other issue in the theatre. Audiences can no more fail to notice whether actors are black or white than whether they are tall, short, fat, thin, bald or hairy. How much it matters in a given play is a thing infinitely variable, and the variables include the nature of the material and the skill and style of the production. 1996-02-19-the-baker-s-wife.source_prefix:

Monday, February 19, 1996

ROBERT CUSHMAN

WRITTEN BY JOSEPH STEIN AND STEPHEN SCHWARTZ Directed by Todd Stewart At the Studio Theatre, Harbourfront, until Feb. 24 Rating: Musical slight but roles charming BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail THERE is a category of Broadway show that devotes much of its energy to presenting cross-sections of some kind of enclosed community, real or fantastic. I think of it as the Merry Villagers Musical. It's an unruly category whose denizens, either sentimental or satirical, include Brigadoon, Plain and Fancy, Anyone Can Whistle, Lil Abner and The Most Happy Fella. The masterpiece of the genre, if you don't count Porgy and Bess, is Fiddler on the Roof, which owes much of its power to the staging of Jerome Robbins and, as is less often noted, to the supremely skillful libretto furnished by Joseph Stein.

1996-02-20-theatre-review-dr-jekyll-and-.source_prefix:
THEATRE REVIEW DR. JEKYLL AND MR. HYDE - A LOVE STORY

Tuesday, February 20, 1996

ROBERT CUSHMAN

Toronto ONT -- Written by James W. Nichol Directed by Neil Munro Starring Les Carlson and David Storch At St. Lawrence Centre until March 16 Rating: Jekyll plus Hyde is one too many One character with two personalities calls for one actor. With two on stage, the essence of a classic duality is lost. BY ROBERT CUSHMAN Special to The Globe and Mail Toronto RIGHT from the start, a horrible thought assailed me. Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde are the most famous double act in fiction. You may talk of Don Quixote and Sancho Panza, Holmes and Watson, Jeeves and Wooster, even Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, but you have to be modestly literate to do so. None of them trip as persistently and proverbially off the common tongue as do the doctor and his double. They did not, of course, reach this exalted state by being buddies; one is an unholy emanation of the other's worst instincts. Robert Louis Stevenson's brilliant fantasy dramatized a psychological phenomenon of which the world was uneasily aware, but for which it lacked a name. He gave us a double-barrelled one.

contact_edits.before: How can we miss the Eagles if they won't go away? And why would anyone pay as much as $250 to see them when they could see vulgar gender bender Peaches at the Guvernment on the same night? The band that gave us Desperado and Hotel California bring its 17th annual farewell tour to the Air Canada Centre tonight (416-870-8000), but, with apologies to Don Henley, you're much better off seeing Peaches - - the abrasive, sometimes bearded Canadian vixen of electroclash and rap. Not for the faint of heart. But then again, those with heart conditions should probably avoid the credit card bills that result from a night with the Eagles. Friday and Saturday, the critically revered Constantines play the Horseshoe (416-598-4226). But, it should be noted, future child star drug casualties Hanson play the Guvernment on Friday, while surf rock refugees Smash Mouth play the same venue Saturday. On second thought, maybe that shouldn't be noted. Forget we even mentioned it. Aaron Wherry

contact_edits.before: Perhaps a month after the Toronto International Film Festival, take comfort in the little festivals -- the kind where you show up and buy a ticket at the door; so civilized -- that crop up in this film-loving town almost every weekend. From tomorrow to Tuesday the 14th, the Royal Cinema hosts the Toronto International Latin Film Festival. Includes Spanish, Portuguese, French and Italian language films on Latin culture, and the vastness of the mandate makes for some intriguing programming. Of note: About Bunuel, a Spanish/ Mexican/ French documentary on Luis Bunuel; Three Nights of a Saturday, a black comedy set in Santiago during a pivotal soccer match; and Condor Crux: The Legend, the first full-length computer animated film to come out of Argentina. For scheduling, check www.tilff.com. Royal Cinema, 608 College St. Ticketing: 416-364- 3131. Katrina Onstad

contact_edits.before: A barely dramatized memoir -- one of those plays in which the characters' main claim on our attention is that they are related to the author. Marie-Lynn Hammond stands centre-stage and recalls her two Montreal grandmothers: Anglo society gal Elsie and poor Catholic mother-of-10 Corinne. Parochial, and linked by whiny, finger- wagging songs, but with excellent performances by Maria Ricossa as Elsie and especially Deborah Lalonde-Grover as Corrine. (Artword Theatre, 75 Portland St., 416-366-7723. Until May 9.)

contact_edits.before: Jackie Richardson as the jazz, blues and cabaret singer Alberta Hunter and Montego Gover as everyone else make this an enjoyable evening. But the show retains its stunning indifference to (and ignorance of) the facts of Hunter's life and music, from the Chicago clubland of the teens and '20s to her octogenarian comeback in the '70s. The guiding principle seems to be that any old song will do, while the non-musical scenes are crummy. (New Yorker Theatre, 651 Yonge St., 416-872-1111. Until June 6.)

contact_edits.before: In Paula Wing's play, Jamie is a 10-year-old whose problem, like most people's, is fear. His parents are constantly splitting up, and menace lurks in the corners of his apartment building -- menace puzzlingly but effectively represented by skulking figures out of film noir. The wisecracking, wheelchair-bound landlady recruits Jamie for her private espionage schemes: She's frightened, too. A compelling, intelligent play and production. (Lorraine Kimsa Theatre for Young People, 165 Front St. E., 416-862-2222. Until May 9.)

contact_edits.before: Karl Valentin was a German comedian who flourished until the Second World War, which he more or less sat out. Peter Froehlich, an authoritative performer but not a great clown, recreates his routines, aided by the sympathetic Nicola Lipman as his performance partner, Liesl Karlstadt, and the musical Peter Tiefenbach. It's an interesting evening but it doesn't have much urgency. (Tarragon Theatre, 30 Bridgeman Ave., 416-531-1827. Runs until May 30.)

The remains are those of the female victims of a serial killer at large in Edmonton, while love is sought in some form by each of the play's seven characters. Performances are mostly fine, with Damien Atkins impressive and enjoyable as David, who gets all the best lines and goes the longest journey. contact_edits.before: Unity, Sask., is the site of Kevin Kerr's play about an influenza epidemic that took millions of lives just as the First World War was ending. The play is an unfocused fantasia on the subject of sex (frustrated) and death (achieved); some variations on the theme are, so to speak, left over from the war. Despite a few sweet or piercing moments, the fictitious characters are so many marionettes, all awaiting their turn to die or mourn. Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace, 16 Ryerson Ave., 416-504-7529. Runs until May 16.

contact_edits.before: Mel Brooks's film was a satire. His stage show is a celebration of the great gleaming entertainment machine that used to be the American musical. Susan Stromans direction keeps the show moving and breathing, and her comic choreography is her best. Brooks's pastiche music is unassumingly accurate -- better, surprisingly, than his lyrics. The Canadian cast is top-notch. "If you've got it, flaunt it." They have, and they do, and we love it. (Canon Theatre, 244 Victoria St., 416-872-1212. Open run.)

contact_edits.before: Obsidian Theatre's production does no favours to George Boyd's play, Consecrated Ground, about the governmental expropriation of Africville, a Halifax slum-ghetto, in 1965. The author's indignation sets off some sparks, but the action halts and hops from one scene to another. The direction is limp, and Kevin Hanchard is the only actor to play with consistent force and fluency. (Factory Theatre, 125 Bathurst St., 416-504-9971. Runs until May 30.)

contact_edits.before: Second City's "55th Sketch Comedy Revue" has the series best title in recent memory but is the worst show. Loud and angry political satire is promised, but it boils down to anti-Bush jokes that are as lazy and repetitive as what they're lampooning. The good stuff includes numbers about gay maternity leave, office psychobabble and Rochester ("the Winnipeg of America"). The performers, as usual, are fine; but they're also the writers. (Tim Sims Playhouse, 56 Blue Jays Way, 416-343-0011. Open run.)

contact_edits.before: Rick Roberts's play offers variations on themes from Samuel Beckett. Man One and Man Two are both very old; One (a very fine Oliver Dennis) is flying a kite, which gets stuck in a tree; Two (a piping Marjorie Campbell) has an assignation with a younger woman, and would like One to leave. It's about the indignities of old age, taken to metaphorical extremes, and has some tedious passages and some with real resonance. (Tarragon Theatre Backspace, 30 Bridgeman Ave., 416-531-1827. Run ends tomorrow.)

Final weekend. An instant classic by Nigerian laureate Wole Soyinka. Yoruba custom dictates that the king's horseman follow his late master in an act of ritual suicide. He's a man whom fate has cast in a tragedy but who often seems to feel he would be more at home in a comedy. The cultural clashes, over two modes of life and two views of death, could hardly be more topical. The play has greatness in it. The less said about the production, the better. (Artword Theatre, 75 Portland St., 416-408-2783. Run ends tomorrow.)

Unfortunately, much else in this "classic American comedy" suggests that those concerned don't trust the play. There are running gags at the expense of the material, and some performances are embarrassingly exaggerated, though the three gamblers who give the play its title make an excellently contrasted trio. (Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, 1-800-511-7429. Runs until October.)

contact_edits.before: A treat. Shaw's comedy, an effortlessly witty hard-edged romance, is given a panoramic production, splendiferously designed, with Jim Mezon and Tara Rosling charting a clear and exhilarating line through the relationship of the professor and the flower-girl, and Simon Bradbury delivering dustman Doolittle's prose arias with superb aplomb. My Fair Lady hasn't killed this play off; there's room for both, and one wouldn't want to be without either. (Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake, 1-800-511-7429. Runs until November.)

contact_edits.before: Eugene O'Neill's one comedy, a gentle one, is a nostalgic piece, recalling family life in "a large small town" in 1904 Connecticut -- O'Neill's boyhood as he would have liked it to have been. His wish- fulfilling dream had, by the end of the Depression, become all of America's. The implicit contrast between fantasy and reality makes the play poignant as well as charming and funny. Joseph Ziegler's production is lovely, with fine work from Norman Browning, as the father. (Courthouse Theatre, Niagara on-the-Lake, 1-800-511-7429)

contact_edits.before: In this period of post-election recovery, we decided to forgo the angry ragings of Marilyn Manson (yesterday at Massey Hall), for the softer sounds of Sufjan Stevens. The quiet singer/songwriter has, perhaps hastily, been lumped in with a number of similar souls as leaders of a new folk. The young man from Michigan became something of a curiosity when his third album, Greetings from Michigan, was touted as the first in a 50-album ode to every American state. Wishful thinking perhaps, but endearing all the same. The follow- up, Seven Swans (released this year), delved deeper into his pursuits of spirituality and storytelling, somehow making God bearable for the usually Christ-phobic indie hipsters. Winning raves from sea to shining sea, he was even hailed as a worthy successor to the dearly departed Elliott Smith. No pressure, though. Stevens plays Lee's Palace tonight. Tickets are $14 (416-532-1598).

contact_edits.before: There are two weeks left in which to catch Hairspray (Princess of Wales, 416-872-1212), a show that's tempting to overrate simply because it's so much fun: fun for the audiences and fun, one imagines, for the bang-up Canadian cast. Anyone who finds this just too frivolous can rest assured that Serious Theatre is still alive and ... well, alive in Toronto. In Omnium Gatherum (CanStage, 416- 872-1111), the New York dinner-party play, terrorism and allied issues are discussed as earnestly as if the diners were so many walking op-ed columns. In No Great Mischief (Tarragon, 416-536- 5018), a family saga set mainly in Cape Breton, the stage is awash in homely local colour. contact_edits.before: Stephen Sondheim has become a cultural icon, so Side by Side by Sondheim, a proselytizing 1976 revue, may have have outlived its historical purpose. It could still be a decent evening's entertainment, but this production is loaded with handicaps, including a coy gentility of approach inherent in the piece itself. Kids who know Aladdin only through the Disney movie may be surprised to learn that the hero had a comic, widowed, cross- dressing mama and she had two funny, incompetent assistants. That may not be authentic Arabian Nights but it's pure English panto, as interpreted in Ross Petty's seasonal transplant, one of his best. Petty himself is, of course, the villain, and in the prologue a down- and-out sheltering in a library; he acts this well. Jennifer Dale is the very sexy librarian. Let us pause to consider this universal fantasy. Now let us move on. Adam Brazier is the charmingly gormless skateboarding hero, who rubs his lamp and gets a wrestler; that's Bret The Hitman" Hart making his acting debut as a genie. Robin Williams he isn't, but at least he's there in the flesh. Until Dec. 31 at the Elgin Theatre. For tickets call 416-872-5555.

contact_edits.before: On the heels of Hotel Rwanda, Hollywood's take on Africa's troubles, comes a screening of a new documentary, Liberia: An Uncivil War, by Jonathan Stack and James Brabazon. Part of the ongoing Hot Docs series, Liberia looks at events in the summer of 2003, when rebels in the west African nation, already in control of 70% of the country, stormed Monrovia. Stack stayed in the capital while Brabazon travelled with the rebels, and what emerges is a balanced, terrifying and sad portrait of a once-proud nation in political tatters. Monrovia, settled by freed American slaves in the 1800s, has long considered itself the little brother of America, but since the end of the Cold War in 1989, relations cooled, and by 2003 little aid was forthcoming from the United States. Liberias president, Charles Taylor, promised to step down once peacekeepers arrived, but no one would send them before a ceasefire. The screening will be followed by a Q&A with Stack. At the Bloor Cinema, 506 Bloor St. W., 7 p.m. More information at 416-203-2155 or www.hotdocs.ca.

contact_edits.before: In Trout Stanley, Claudia Dey delivers a masterwork. Glamorous Grace and quietly desperate Sugar, 30-year old twin sisters, run the town garbage dump and manufacture tragic figurines, respectively. This, without a hint of camp, is a play about people who live at extremes of climate and feeling, joyously written with tense, witty verbal duels and soaring prose arias. Unimprovably acted by Melody A. Johnson, Michelle Giroux and Gord Rand as the titular intruder, who is not a fish. (Factory Theatre, until Feb 8, 416-504-9971.)

contact_edits.before: Now, in the calm after this year's initial storm of Toronto openings, may be the time to look ahead to April and the start of the Stratford and Shaw festivals, when at the very least the weather should be better. The only part of the repertoire to which both organizations habitually stake a claim is that of modern American classics, musical and other. Looking at the other, the dramas: Each festival offers two of them; all four open in June. The Shaw (905- 468-2172; www.shawfest.com) proposes Lillian Hellman's little-seen The Autumn Garden (1951), which is about mature love in Louisiana, and whose distinguished players include Jim Mezon, Goldie Semple, Peter Hutt, Sharry Flett and Patricia Hamilton; Martha Henry directs. William Inges Bus Stop (1955) is known to some as a stage vehicle for Kim Stanley, and to many more as a film vehicle for Marilyn Monroe; Nicole Underhay steps into their shoes and whatever else as the club singer marooned with her fellow travellers in a winter storm. Stratford (1-800-567-1600. www.stratfordfestival.ca) devotes itself in this area exclusively to Tennessee Williams. Richard Monette directs Cat on a Hot Tin Roof, Williams last really famous play, with Cynthia Dale as Maggie the Cat, David Snelgrove as her husband, Brick, and James Blendick as Big Daddy, a role he reprises from the last Stratford production. Sweet Bird of Youth is directed by Miles Potter with a formidable-looking cast: Seana McKenna, Jonathan Goad (currently wowing 'em in A Whistle in the Dark), Michelle Giroux (ditto in Trout Stanley), Scott Wentworth, Dixie Seatle and -- making a long-awaited Stratford return -- Fiona Reid.

contact_edits.before: Its rare enough that teams in organized sport at any level can win 66 games in a row against comparable competition, and rarer still to get an opportunity to witness such a team. But tomorrow night at 8 p.m. at the Tait McKenzie Centre at York University, basketball fans can see the Carleton Ravens, 17-0 this season, winners of the last two Canadian championships and holders of the above-mentioned streak, play the Lions in an Ontario university men's East Division contest. York is perhaps one of the few teams that can claim a realistic chance of winning. The Lions are in second behind the Ravens with a 14-4 record and lost by only three points, 65-62, on the opening weekend of the regular season in Ottawa. Opening the bill, the 9-9 York women play the 3-14 Carleton women at 6 p.m. Ticket information, 416-736-5183.

contact_edits.before: Two of the city's best shows have had their runs extended. The Factory's Trout Stanley is worth seeing for Claudia Deys quirky, witty, image-drenched text, for Eda Holmes taut and imaginative direction and for the boldly expansive performances of Michelle Giroux, Melody Johnson and Gord Rand. It now goes an extra week, until Feb. 13 (416-504-9971). 'da Kink in My Hair will now run at the Princess of Wales until March 6. It's a rare opportunity to see a work that both comes from and speaks for a neighbourhood Toronto community (the Caribbean one) on a big central stage. There are some rough edges in the works transition from smallish play to biggish musical, but the best sections are truthful and vibrant; the very best are searing and joyful (416-872-1212).

contact_edits.before: The Toronto dance community, becalmed throughout January, is surging ahead with a vengeance this week. Brazilian-born Newton Moraes unveils his techno-tribal Lamour en silence at Harbourfront Centre (see story above), while Toronto Dance Theatre convenes its annual choreographic invitational, Four at the Winch, at company headquarters (80 Winchester St., 416-967-1365). True dance connoisseurs, however, will not want to miss the incomparable Peggy Baker in a program of solos featuring live accompaniment by pianist Andrew Burashko and a pair of estimable dancing guests. The middle- aged but lithe Baker, eager to pass on her work, invites former National Ballet star Rex Harrington and modern dance doyenne Sasha Ivanochko to perform her powerful solo, Brute. Sounds like a compelling combination. Betty Oliphant Theatre (404 Jarvis), Saturday at 8 p.m. and Sunday at 4 p.m. Tickets from $22, 416-504- 7529 or at www.artsboxoffice.ca. Michael Crabb

contact_edits.before: Even enthusiasts of American musicals can have their doubts about the extent to which they have taken over the classical theatres in Canada, just as they already had in the U.K. (Not, ironically, in the United States, which doesn't have a classical theatre.) So the appearance of a musical on the mainstage of the Shaw Festival (1- 800-511-7429) -- which has previously kept them pocket-sized -- may be regarded as a two-edged sword. Still, the show itself is one of the best: Gypsy, lyrics by Stephen Sondheim and book by Arthur Laurents. Nora McLellan, who has given good Ethel Merman in the past, takes on the Merm's greatest role, the archetypal battleaxe stage mother, in a production by Jackie Maxwell. There's a smaller show as well, the return, from two seasons ago, of the Bertolt Brecht-Kurt Weill Happy End, German of course but set in an imaginary U.S., with some of the duo's best songs, if hardly their best script. Stratford (1-800-567-1600), meanwhile, offers another Sondheim, the festival's first attempt at a show for which he wrote both music and lyrics, the late masterpiece Into the Woods. More populistically, if there is such a word, there's Hello Dolly, which Noel Coward memorably described as a show he didn't like but hugely enjoyed. It's a common reaction. Dolly herself is usually cast with a personality whose mere appearance at the top of that staircase gets the crowd cheering. But the show is based on a distinguished play (The Matchmaker), and Stratford has cast a real actress-who- can-sing, Lucy Peacock. This may be a first. It should certainly be an event.

contact_edits.before: The play bears a fortuitous resemblance to Pedro Almodovar's Volver; both have estranged generations of women finding reconciliation, skeletons in family cupboards (more numerous and extreme in the movie) and a mother with a musical past, though the Spanish one's talent is for singing rather than dancing. It's unfair to compare a beginning playwright with a brilliant director at the height of his powers: The liquid movie is obviously in a different class from the lumpy play. In one respect, though, Hernandez' vision is more inclusive than Almodovar's; it finds a place for men, and -- Singkil revisionism notwithstanding --a generous one. Both are fundamentally warm-hearted works, but the play has structural cracks that make it feel chilly. - Until Jan. 28. 416-504-9971

contact_edits.before: What else? Spectators are issued with little green light-sticks that they obediently wave in the air. Audiences (and not just for this show): Refuse participation. You have nothing to gain but your self-respect. Arlene Phillips choreography might be excused on the grounds that those who execute it are supposed to be robots, but couldn't the robots have been more imaginatively programmed? Elton's script does run to a few good jokes, all of them crammed into one scene in the second act and entrusted to a pickled hippie, played with pleasing relish by Jack Langeduk. But even he is only there to fulfill the show's main purpose, which is to make a narcissistic generation feel nostalgically good about itself. - We Will Rock You plays until May 27. It's to the credit of Robert Chafe, the author, that though the play tells a story that could clearly not have been invented, it doesn't feel like a documentary. Its first act, though, feels repetitive. In a rapid but protracted series of vignettes we see Nurse Bennett, the very sound and picture of a no- nonsense angel of mercy, working most hours, conquering local prejudice, local superstition and local hearts. A local heart of which she makes a particular conquest belongs to Angus, who manages to interrupt her professional ministrations just long enough to propose and be accepted. Probably it didn't happen quite like that, but its charming to pretend it did. Act 2 slows down and is shorter; it concentrates on an injury to Angus's brother and an epic sleigh ride to get him to proper treatment and avoid amputation. It's this exploit that seems to have sealed the Bennett legend. Honours followed, and even a real road. Jillian Keiley, a legendary Canadian director whose work has hardly been seen here, delivers an unobtrusively virtuoso production. Chairs and a table are arranged and re-arranged to suggest the various locations, but the focus is still firmly on the acting. Deidre Gillard-Rowlings finds exactly the right brisk rhythm for Myra and sticks to it; she also sticks to the same brisk pace and here we might have used some variation. Darryl Hopkins makes Angus the same sympathetic helpmate on stage as he must have been in life; and Robert Wyatt Thorne and Melanie Caines fill all the other roles to near-perfection. - Revisited runs through April 19 at the Brigantine Room, York Quay Centre, 416-973- 4000; Tempting Providence runs through April 22 at the Factory Theatre, 416-504-9971.

contact_edits.before: The second play, Sea Change -- "a city park, decades from today" - - is a kind of long-range prequel to the first. The two pieces are in fact linked by a single object, a copy of Reader's Digest. (I'm not telling how.) Things are materially better than they will later become, but the rot has already set in; technology is omnipresent, individuality is eroding and life is cheap. Ironically, the person who feels least at home in a world where people have computers literally in the palm of their hands is a former video-game designer. He's been overtaken. He has billion-dollar election- rigging secrets in his briefcase, but he's no match for two young women: a peddler of uplifting pamphlets who can change identities in an instant and a gun-toting adventuress. There are any number of twists and turns. This spy-spoof is less imaginative satire than its companion piece but brisker entertainment. Richings manages to be taut and bemused at the same time, and the two women are all kinds of tough. I blame both plays, or the worlds of both plays, on global warming, as I am surely meant to do. Warm is the new cool. - Until April 29. Call 416-504- 7529 for ticket information.

contact_edits.before: This is altogether a lighter production than the original. (Lighter in the most basic sense--it is, if I can trust my memory, far more brightly lit.) This has something to do with time, something probably with the logical French language and the ironic French temperament. But, if the delivery is light, it carries a heavy freight. Konga, dreaming awkwardly of his future, has wonderful moments of delicate comedy, pipe in his mouth, assuming a manager's pose. The photography theme is constant and vital to the plot. It's a service that Styles, reflecting on early ghastly experiences with family groups ("37 New Brighton smiles on the same photo--never again") has, without knowing it, been setting himself up as a saviour. Habib Dembele gives him a joyous, elfin quality and balances it with good-humoured man-of-the-world exasperation as Sizwe's friend and other rescuer, the man who exhorts him to grab at salvation, even when he finds it literally lying in the gutter. Between them, these actors create a world for us. The play is little like Fugard's unaided works, which are drier and also duller; it's full of pungent detail, shrugged or mocked at, understated to shock. Dembele plays several roles, Konga only one, but they both give the impression of enormous versatility and enormous mutual trust. The level of contact here--actor to actor, actors to audience -- is remarkable. Brook, in the simplest way, has done it again. - Until April 22. Call 416-973-4000 for ticket information.

contact_edits.before: One last subtlety:When Lear at the end says "and my poor fool is hanged," audiences have always taken for granted that he means the Fool, while the unsentimental insist that he means Cordelia. Bedford has it both ways. His Lear is confused; he thinks that he means the Fool, then you can see him jerked back to reality as he remembers that the actual victim, there dead beside him, is someone ever more precious. "Break heart, I prithee break" says Kent; and it does. So, I think, will yours. - King Lear is in repertory at the Stratford Festival until Oct. 28. For tickets, call 1-800-567-1600 or visit www.stratfordfestival.ca

contact_edits.before: The staging (Glenn Casale) and sets (John Iacovelli) are very makeshift. Rachel York has charm and spunk as Guenevere, while showing again that it's impossible to play this role without sounding exactly like Julie Andrews, not only in the range and colour of her singing, but in the roguishness of her speech. That said, her singing of Before I Gaze at You Again, not previously a song to which I've ever paid much attention, is the evening's high point. An actor with the unlikely name of Time Winters gets all the available fun out of King Pellinore, a transplanted English clubman who arrives at court in search of the Questing Beast, like (he says) all the Pellinores before him, and then forgets about it for the rest of the show. He's fortunate, for purely technological reasons, in not having to sing. We have suffered much recently from overbearing sound systems; now here's one that's underbearing. It makes everyone, from the vibrant Ms. York to the modest Mr. York, sound as if their vocal cords have been wrapped in cotton wool. - Camelot runs until June 30. For more information call 416-872-2262.

contact_edits.before: Germaine Greer has a book coming out about Anne Hathaway that, she says, proclaims the marriage to have been happy and Anne to have been practically Shakespeare's muse. I don't see where the evidence can come from, but then I can't see much evidence to the contrary, either. The trajectory Thiessen presents -- a canny but trusting woman fighting off disillusion, but finally thrust into it --makes sense on its own terms, but the development is sketchy. But there's enough to enable Seana McKenna to shine. The production has her going up and down a flight of steps more often than seems necessary, but she is completely in command of her own highs and lows. She encompasses roguishness, sensuality, wit --both defensive and aggressive -- and scalding pain, neither underplaying nor overdoing. The performance may justify the choice of play: You will know, coming out, that McKenna is a superlative actress. But you probably knew that going in as well. - In repertory through to Sept. 20. I don't see where the evidence can come from, but then I can't see much evidence to the contrary, either. The trajectory Thiessen presents -- a canny but trusting woman fighting off disillusion, but finally thrust into it --makes sense on its own terms, but the development is sketchy. But there's enough to enable Seana McKenna to shine. The production has her going up and down a flight of steps more often than seems necessary, but she is completely in command of her own highs and lows. She encompasses roguishness, sensuality, wit --both defensive and aggressive -- and scalding pain, neither underplaying nor overdoing. The performance may justify the choice of play: You will know, coming out, that McKenna is a superlative actress. But you probably knew that going in as well. - In repertory through to Sept. 20. visit Stratford-festival. ca.

contact_edits.before: The show may be stale but the production and performances are surprisingly fresh. Jeff Calhoun's direction is smooth, Lisa Stevens' choreography is energetic and Kenneth Foy's sets are excellent -- with their rows and rows of overhead lights, they are impressively spacious and make institutional architecture look like a good idea. John Jeffrey Martin and Arielle Jacobs are an appealing Troy and Gabriella, the only two people in nthe show who resemble real human beings. The rest of the cast don't get that chance, but they caricature with vigour. Chandra Lee Schwartz and Bobby List are as amusing a pair of terrible twins as anyone has a right to expect, given their material, and Ellen Harvey as Ms. Darbus does a very good Carol Burnett; even her passion for the drama is weirdly, indeed alarmingly, believable. Nice too is Olivia Ogama as the timid composer of the show-within-the-show which, for all we are allowed to see or hear of it, may be a masterpiece. (Though, on the basis of the one song we do hear, probably not.) Like everyone else, she gets to pair off at the end; in her case, it's with the school's resident newsreader, who spends the entire show making hysterically cheery announcements and mysteriously gets to the end of the evening without somebody strangling him. I notice that though the casting is proudly multicultural, the actual couplings are strictly intra- racial. And though Ryan, too, is allowed to find a partner, that encounter is kept very coy and upstage. School fiction, in any genre, is always aimed at an audience younger than the characters it depicts -- nobody finds their own contemporaries glamorous --but in this show, the gap yawns wider than ever before. - High School Musical runs until Sept. 23 at the Princess of Wales Theatre. For tickets, call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish.com.

contact_edits.before: Jennifer H. Capraru, the director, clearly lays out the play's emotional geography but runs into problems, probably not of her own making, with the physical. A site-specific production raises high expectations of scenic realism; otherwise, why not set the play on a conventional stage? Here we have a living-room that changes without warning into a bedroom, and a basement that seems to be on the same level as the rest of the house. When you stop believing in a play's spatial dynamic, you start having problems with its character dynamics as well. This aside, the design is excellent; as might be expected, since it's by Tamara Marie Kucheran, who's also responsible for the Passe Muraille revival of The Drawer Boy and, last year at Stratford, for the gorgeous Fanny Kemble. The play's title is a poser; it doesn't acquire any relevance until the play is almost over, and it seems arbitrary and sentimental when it does. But it isn't quite the end; and when Ferry's Kenny shuffles off into the night, leaving chaos behind him, he moves you not as a figure on a sociologist's graph, but as a complex, inexplicable human being. - Performances run through Nov. 18. For tickets, call 416-460-9306.

contact_edits.before: There's a well-staged fight, but for the most part Leslie O'Dell's production can make the play nothing but dull. Christopher Stanton, once past his early contortions, gives a decent account of Will, but Mark McGrinder's Sam is done in by a continuous vocal smirk, which is intended to convey ambiguous cheerfulness; his attempts at bolstering his companion's morale sound positively nannyish. Perhaps, if a playwright wants to get us thinking about modern warfare, he should choose a different conflict. It's true that 1914-18 was the entrance to the chamber of horrors in which we still live, but dramatically and otherwise it's been done -- to use a rather too appropriate phrase -- to death. There have been innumerable literary and dramatic treatments of this war, and it's hard to add anything new. At any rate, it hasn't happened here. It's cruel, but true, that the best comment on this play is its title. - Performances run through Nov. 10. For tickets, call 416-866-8666.

contact_edits.before: The one unquestionably triumphant thing about this show is its look. Ken MacDonald's set and Charlotte Dean's costumes transport us to a vanished world where doctors made house calls in evening dress, or indeed to a vanished world where doctors made house calls. Everything that isn't explicitly ghostly is done in shades of grey; the cups in the china cabinet match the upholstery on the sofa. In scale and proportion, this is a paragon among country-house settings, majestic without being overpowering. At the end, when the ghosts turn to poltergeists, the set even gets to do a turn of its own, with furnishings flying all over the place. It could even afford to go on longer and more violently; this is a rare example of Panych erring on the side of restraint. Overall, there's a whiff of superior summer theatre about this winter show, starting with the choice of play. It's Soulpepper punching below its weight. - Blithe Spirit runs until Dec. 15. For tickets and show information, call 416-866-8666.

contact_edits.before: Salt-Water Moon is a slighter play than Leaving Home, but it's also more likeable and has fewer loose ends. Its principal weakness is that though we hear, evocatively, about the decline of the local fisheries and, less evocatively, about the shadowing trauma of the recent war, neither theme seems to have entered into the blood and being of the couple we actually see. It's background, part of the "this is our country, look at it" aesthetic that underlies most of French's plays, not to mention others of the time, such as David Fennario's Balconville. It was probably a necessary phase for Canadian drama to pass through, but it's difficult to imagine the plays being taken as seriously anywhere else. But here is here, and the plays have cut a distinctive new panel in Soulpepper's tapestry. A company whose repertory roams the world needs to come home now and then. - Salt-Water Moon runs until Jan. 31. Call 416-866-8666 for more information.

This brings us to "An Iraqi Mother," who also has a real-life analogue, though one likely to be unknown to
most: Nehrjas Al Saffarh, who survived her torture under Saddam only to be inadvertently killed by the U.S. (Her home was bombed in the first Gulf War.) Arsinee Khanjian is bland and monotonous when setting her character up for us, but develops considerable intensity when describing her actual ordeal. She has the misfortune of being handed the play's most pretentious
element: a mystical dream of future peace and reconciliation that hardly measures up to the hideous realities that have gone before. The ending also suffers from a forced attempt by author and director to draw all three characters together; the first two are mute audience to the third though their reactions remain inscrutable. Having them all talk about their respective journeys "through the looking-glass" doesn't do much for artistic unity either. These are three shards, wrenching ones, from the tragedy of Iraq. There is no way that they, or any other three, can add up a to a full picture. - Palace of the End runs until Feb. 23. For tickets, call 416-368-3110 or visit canstage.com.

contact_edits.before: The Russian Play is a scintillating exercise in style (owing more to Chekhov's short stories than his plays, whatever the script says) which also manages to be a moving meditation on poverty, oppression and love. I have now seen Michelle Monteith's performance as Sonya three times, and I can't say that it has improved; it was perfect the first time and it still is, impossibly mature, both technically and emotionally, in its instant switches from sardonic narrator to trusting heroine and back again. That the two women are in fact one is only revealed at the end, though I can't see any point in keeping that secret. As before, Monteith gets strong support from Shawn Campbell and Aaron Willis as the two (married) men in her life, which is more than you can say of Sonya herself; one, a poor gravedigger, breaks her heart, the other, a rich factory-owner, breaks her body. Also as before, and also invaluable in their contributions to matters of atmosphere and tension, are Tom Howell's violin-playing and Kimberly Purtell's cruelly acute lighting. The play's scale, and its key, may be minor but the overall achievement, under Natasha Mytnowych's direction, is major. - The Russian Play/ Essay runs until Feb. 17. Call 416-504-9971 for more information.

contact_edits.before: The production, by the star's wife, Donna Feore, gets off to a mystifying start with a small modern boy (played by their son) trying on a cadet's costume. As a framing device, it's unnecessary, and anyway never appears again. Once that's over, Mrs. Feore surrounds Mr. Feore with an excellent staging that gets the Festival platform swirling with action, as you might expect from an expert choreographer, but also fills it with intelligence. She shows you where to look and gives you things worth looking at and listening to. She only misreads one moment, when she has Wayne Best, otherwise admirable as the protagonist's friend Le Bret, shout his sympathy over Cyrano's rejection by the adored Roxane rather than confide it. Amanda Lisman, as the lady in question, simpers more than a bluestocking should, and their common enemy de Guiche is a more complex figure than the pantomime villain supplied by John Vickery. But there are some very nice small performances: Douglas E. Hughes as a drunken versifier; Robert Persichini doubling as a ham actor whom Cyrano drives from the stage and as the Gascons' commanding officer; Martha Farrell as a refreshment vendor whose adoration would strike Cyrano in a heap if only he could see beyond his nose. John Stead has arranged a fine duel and a great battle. Occasional passages are spoken in the original French, which may not be strictly logical, but is no less so than Shakespeare's anglophone Julius Caesar expiring with Latin on his lips. Besides, Burgess himself admitted that there could be no English translation for Cyrano's own dying word which is, and remains, panache. Which is also a fair summary of the whole show. - Cyrano de Bergerac is in repertory through Nov. 1. Call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.cafor tickets and information.

The author lays out for herself the task of dramatizing the terrible day as it would have appeared to these people -- the casual turning on of the TV, the frantic telephoning that would be comic in another context, the overwhelming but temporary relief--and she brings it off with total conviction. A rather similar challenge confronts the actor who plays Jean, who only comes onstage halfway through, after what I can only describe as one hell of a retrospective buildup. This, too, is brilliantly met, with Jeff Irving conveying the essence of a walking nightmare, shifting between blankness and hysteria. The actual details of the massacre are sparingly mentioned, but they're omnipresent; we catch glimpses of them in Kathleen's bitter acknowledgment of how many lives were wrecked, even her irrational jealousy of how some other victims were buried. Christmas is a recurring image in the play. There could be many other ways of dramatizing that one horrific December day, but it's hard to believe that there could be one more effective. - In Toronto until May 17. A dual-levelled set, with a third layer occasionally dropped in for people to die on, conjures up both a feudal court in which the rulers prefer to keep the starving ruled down below and out of sight, and the shifts between dream and reality in a beautiful, mysterious work. Maybe the mystery turned off the first-night audience, whose response was phenomenally tepid by operatic standards. But even if diva-worship (and divoworship) is your main thing, you should be amply rewarded by Russell Braun's Pelleas, Isabel Bayrakdarian's Melisande, and above all -- certainly in acting terms -- by the great Pavlo Hunka as the jealous Golaud, working wonders with an anguished pianissimo. - Sexual Practices of the Japanese runs through May 18 at the Factory Theatre. O'Haire apart, the best things about the show are the ironic presence of Marni Nixon, the celebrated vocal ghost who dubbed Audrey Hepburn in the Fair Lady film, in the non-singing role of Mrs. Higgins, and the un-ironic excellence with which she plays it. Walter Charles has his moments as Colonel Pickering, though he's too little the gentleman, too much the buffoon. Distressingly further down the same road is Justin Bohon's Freddy, so exaggerated a twit that, though he has the voice to sing On the Street Where You Live, he completely forfeits the right. Anthony Ward's sets make an evocative job of Covent Garden (where the production has its most charming moments) and an imposing one of Higgins' monumentally book-lined study. His establishment is, as usual, impossibly large for a mere professor of phonetics: I counted four maids, two footmen and a housekeeper. Broadway has always been more starry-eyed about the British class system than Britain itself was. Which, though I'm not complaining, is the difference in a nutshell between the incurably romantic My Fair Lady and its impenitently satirical source. - My Fair Lady plays until May 31. For ticket information, call 416-872-1111.

She, who for years has paid the piper, can finally make him dance to her tune. Each of them is comically oblivious of the other's values and modes of operation; they do know that they're in a life-and-death struggle. Rather less subtle are the setting that Britta Gerecke has dreamed up for Annie's stronghold, full of poles but short on walls, and James Fisher's supposedly spooky sound-score, which seems to think that the play is still a movie. The two forms have different ways of creating suspense, and what's effective in one can be ludicrous in the other. Which reminds me: The CanStage program note says Misery is the only work of King's to have made the journey from page to screen to stage. contact_edits.before: The Avon stage can't match the vistas of the shows previous airing at the Festival Theatre. Philosophically I approve of the decision to restrict musicals to the proscenium house, but I have to confess that The Music Man was one of two shows -- Fiddler on the Roof, also about a town, was the other -- that justified the epic look. Still, Patrick Clark's sets bring striped-suit ice-cream-parlour America to delectable life, and the population is by and large terrific. It includes such surprise musical casting as Sara Topham, doing some earnestly bedraggled hoofing, and Michelle Fisk, wonderfully warm, sharp and tuneful as the heroine's mother. Those more accustomed to this kind of thing include Eddie Glen, an expert sidekick; a formidable colla voce quartet (Laird Mackintosh, Shawn Wright, Jonathan Monro, Marcus Nance); and a malapropping Mayor (Lee MacDougall) who, like the hero he opposes, is delightful but a little short on threat. There are also some more-than-bearable children, headed by Christopher Van Hagen as the lisping boy who learns to sing Gary, Indiana. He is key to the redemptive ending, which comes a bit sudden in this production but casts a glow anyway. The Music Man beat West Side Story at the 1958 Tonys. Historians usually reckon this to be an injustice, but I'm not so sure. - The Music Man is in repertory through Nov. 1 at the Avon Theatre, Stratford. Call 1-800-567-1600 for more information.
