The thinking seems to have been that a bleeding political situation, a martyrdom, and an autobiographical paper trail should add up to a play. Some of the best parts are the letters she reads from her proud but worried parents; it's good to hear other points of view and theirs -- trying cheerfully to be supportive, but leaking any number of doubts -- are very recognizable. The piece goes from engaging to monotonous to baffling to gripping-- the baffling part being a pre-climactic retrospective detour -- the only point at which the play makes its heroine seem self-indulgent. It recovers itself to plunge into something like tragedy, with a ground-down Rachel's despairing conclusion that there may be more evil in the world than good; Jillard rises thrillingly to the challenge. She recovers her optimism, which I suppose means that the play does. But I'm not so sure; her end -- which, of course, we've been anticipating all evening -- still comes shockingly fast. Just one death, of course, in a world that's full of them, and no more to be lamented than anyone else's, but the theatre doesn't work that way. We suffer with those whom we've seen suffer, and here, whatever news she herself may bring of others, there's only one of them. - My Name is Rachel Corrie plays through June 29 at the Tarragon Extra Space. contact_edits.before: That leaves the gods, who speak a prologue that's bland to them, but bitterly ironic for everyone else. Greek tragedy draws on a vast mythological corpus: The writers could light up parts of the canvas as they chose, confident that their audience could fill gaps and draw conclusions. It's not so much subtext as ubertext. Here we have Poseidon and Athena, miffed that the Greeks haven't been making them the proper sacrifices, capriciously plotting their downfall, which will happen after the play ends. Poseidon, god of the ocean, is in naval uniform, and the two of them appear to be hanging out on the gangway of some beached battleship. I find the Greek view of divinity, Euripides' anyway, very plausible. It's the only theology that answers that old question about bad things happening to good people. The gods have the power but, with all that immortality to play with, they long ago got bored with us. In another view, they are us magnified, mainly for the worse. The Trojan Women is maybe the prime example of a play that's great without being, in any conventional sense, good. It has no plot, only episodes. It ends with Troy in flames: the only possible climax but halfheartedly depicted here. If you want to know what burning Troy was really like then, in a Stratford season full of cross-references, stroll along the Avon and catch the First Player's speech in Hamlet. - The Trojan Women runs until Oct. 5. For tickets and information, call 1-800-567-1600 or visit www.stratfordfestival.ca.

I have no idea what Patrick McManus is doing with the page Biondello, for whom he looks both too old and too upscale. Still, what with Randy Hughson, Jeff Lillico and Juan Chioran as rival suitors (Tom, Dick and Harry in the Cole Porter translation) the stage is alive with good actors clinging fiercely to their author, their director and their own instincts. Best of the lot is Stephen Ouimette as father Baptista, giving a squirm of incredulous delight at getting his problem daughter off his hands. Santo Loquasto's set is a handsome complement to the spare modern lines of his Hamlet. contact_edits.before: Now for the good stuff. Some of the attitudes, under Ron Jenkins' direction, are very impressive. Marie Nychka, the choreographer, has staged a wild ball. Much of the singing is muggy, but Michael Scholar Jr., as the diabolic tempter named Peg Leg, cuts through the haze with a ringing solo that warms up the theatre while chilling the blood. Rachael Johnston is marvellous as the heroine, especially when sharing a duet with her intended, he hiding under her skirts, she -- we have to assume -- standing on his shoulders. (This makes hers a literally towering performance.) Finally, within sight of the end, there's a slow-motion death-fall, hilarious and horrific at once, that comes as close as anything I've seen to making manifest the inexorable. It should invade the dreams of everyone who sees it. - The Black Rider runs until Nov. 16. Call 416-531-1827 for ticket and information.

contact_edits.before: Fathers and husbands are kept strictly off stage; the one male actor, Anthony Bekenn, is billed as the symbolic Rat-Catcher but actually appears as a series of officials -- German and English, terrifying or benevolent or in-between -- whom he renders as a series of neat music-hall sketches. These include a wartime postman, mentally lumping Jews with Germans as undesirable aliens and refusing to hear the difference. (This does make a point.) Cameron Porteous, perhaps in reference to the triple time-scheme, has designed a three-arched set that works well for the several scenes that are set in railway stations (with announcements recorded, I suspect, by the director himself ), less well for the more numerous scenes that are supposed to go on in confined spaces like the all-important attic. There are also projections, which are helpful in letting us know where we are but are not especially atmospheric; at the preview I attended, they vanished temporarily due to a computer breakdown, and I don't think that the play suffered much from their absence. I suspect that this play would work best in an intimate theatre with a minimum of design. - Kindertransport is at the Harold Green Theatre until Nov. 23. For tickets and information call 416-366-7723 or visit hgjewishtheatre.com.

contact_edits.before: They're less firmly rooted than in Whistle, because the text gives them less help. As in the film, you're left wondering what it's all for. Are we only here to see, yet again, the bourgeoisie exposed, the elders rotten, the youngers maimed? Probably yes. These characters don't just have skeletons in their closets; they're skeletons themselves. But they certainly rattle with style. Eric Peterson's Helge is more tetchy than tyrannical, if he carried more weight, the play might. Rosemary Dunsmore, though, is superb as his wife, alternately soothing and goading her offspring in a set speech dripping with poisoned politesse. (It's the high point of the play as it was of the film.) Allan Hawco and Philip Riccio, the company's founders, again play brothers, Hawco weak and vicious (last time he was strong and vicious), Riccio an ambiguous avenger. Caroline Cave is rather wasted as Michael's wife, who gives near as good as she gets but has to give most of it early. Tara Rosling transforms herself as Helene; as her nerves go, she seems more and more like a Nordic Janice Soprano. And so it goes, down a fine line that includes Earl Pastko's implacable maitre d' and Nicholas Campbell's understandably depressed tycoon. The entire cast is on red alert. This is about as close as we'll get to pure theatre, with all the limitations that implies and all the excitement. - Festen runs until Dec. 13 at the Berkeley Street Theatre. For ticket information, call 416-368-3110.

contact_edits.before: Weidman's script doesn't overstress the story's resonance as a representative American fable, but it's inescapably there, especially now. Sondheim's score, as intelligent and exploratory as expected, combines jagged with jaunty; it also includes a bewitching long-lined ballad (The Best Thing That Ever Has Happened) unlike anything in his previous work. But he hasn't got as deeply inside his characters as usual. It's far more Addison's show than it's Wilson's -- the opening number is about him -- but in the end, we don't know whether he's his brother's victim or the architect (sorry) of his own misfortune. If it is both, the proportions aren't clear. I doubt, though, that this is the end of the road for Road Show. There's too much gold there, too much bounce, for some theatre not to try it again. - Road Show is at the Public Theater in New York City until Dec. 28. Call 212-967-7555 for tickets and information.

contact_edits.before: A Christmas Carol is worth the price just to see Joseph Ziegler's Ebenezer kicking off his slippers in an ecstasy of joyous reformation; his final rapprochement with Oliver Dennis's crown prince of Cratchits is a heart-warming bonus. Who knew being good could be so much fun? Ziegler's Scrooge is beautifully of a piece; the seeds of humour, if not of good humour, are sown in his early extravagant misanthropy, while his encroaching pain at the sight of opportunities past is very moving. Other welcome returning veterans are John Jarvis's quartet of spirits and Patrick Galligan's incorrigibly cheerful nephew, with Maggie Huculak as an assortment of wenches and crones. In terms of overall ensemble, CanStage cannot on this occasion be faulted. But Soulpepper has the soul. - It's a Wonderful Life runs until Dec. 20. Call 416-368-3110 for tickets and information. contact_edits.before: The hostage-takers are kept offstage, like a collective Godot though one whose appearance is dreaded rather than desired. We don't even hear much about them. Here the play cheats; it may be the captors' strategy to keep the captives physically in the light (it's never switched off) and mentally in the dark (they don't even know what day it is) but they must have said something. They must be making demands of some kind, or why take hostages at all? But the characters say nothing about it, apparently keeping quiet for our benefit. We don't even know if they've been physically ill-treated; there are bruises on Ferry's legs but they're never explained or even referred to. The tensions and resolutions between the cellmates are finely dramatized, their ongoing fight with their jailers not so much: a limitation that's frustrating but that may also, paradoxically, be a strength. There is a fourth voice written into the play, that of Ella Fitzgerald, whose recording of the almost title song (the Gershwins called it Someone to Watch Over Me) is both Edward's choice of imaginary Desert Island Disc and a key to the theme of both play and production: interdependence. - Someone Who'll Watch Over Me is at the Berkeley Street Theatre Upstairs in Toronto until Dec. 13. Call 416-368-3110 for tickets and information.

contact_edits.before: I have few complaints, though, about the performance. Ruth Madoc-Jones' direction is supple and fluid, the myriad transitions excellently handled with much credit to Kimberly Purtell's bare set and bold, sensitive lighting. Of the players, Dawson herself is better at timing her lines than exploring what's beneath them; it's unfortunate, too, that she has to make much of the running in the first quarter of the evening. (I doubt if it was meant to be The Tracy Dawson Show, but it does come on that way.) Powell does unobtrusively and resourcefully well, especially with the night's first monologue. Healey explores, endearingly, many shades of rumpled; at one point he had me convinced that he'd changed the colour of his hair, though all he'd really done was muss it up a little. Dodd shows off the greatest range, from rage to loss to (occasional) glee, and hits each unfussily on the nose; I've never thought of her as a revue performer, and I doubt if she has either, but she has the economy and versatility for it. Some of the scenes -- I almost said numbers -- do echo or complete others, but this doesn't add up to structure. It's as if a Second City running gag were being asked, single-handedly, to repeal the law of diminishing returns - Them And Us Runs until Jan. 31. Call 416-504-7529 for more information.

contact_edits.before: The classroom provides the most drama, the most comedy, and -- whatever your background or gender -- the sharpest recognition. These primary-school kids seem to have the same teacher in every grade, a Miss Campbell, a sentimental battleaxe with a revisionist view of the Massacre of Glencoe, the 1692 atrocity in which, with encouragement from the English, the Campbell clan slaughtered the MacDonald clan in their beds. Literally, as the MacDonalds were their guests at the time. Miss Campbell, true to her family pride, believes that her ancestors have been much misjudged, and that the MacDonalds, always a shifty race, had it coming. My own observation is that the mutual suspicion may well persist to this day, between those who love soup and those who love burgers. As luck would have it, there is a David MacDonald in the class who, with his runny nose and attention deficit, reminds Elsa, who is nonetheless his only protector, of a troll. The show's finest scene is a singing contest at which the rich bitchette acquits herself atrociously, the despised David huskily but truly, Elsa herself outlandishly with windmill gestures and Adelle, tastefully disregarding all the direction Elsa has tried to give her, quite beautifully. Miss Campbell renders true judgment, thereby overcoming all her prejudices, except the unshakable one in favour of the poetry of Robert Burns. (Elsa's feelings about her friend's success are, not surprisingly, mixed, and drive her temporarily into the arms of the snobs.) Singing badly when you can sing well is really hard but Ardal -- without accompaniment, mind you -- makes all four vocal performances completely convincing and melts us with the last as surely as Adelle melts Miss Campbell. It's the crown of a virtuoso performance. She has every right to fancy herself. - You Fancy Yourself is at Theatre Passe Muraille Backspace until Feb. 14. Call 416-504-7529 for tickets and information.

As a director, he confronts a fearsome task with limited resources: The choreography (by Hari Krishnan) is more dutiful than beguiling, though Itai Erdal's lighting can be magical, especially when summoning a slow dawn. The cast is mixed, in both background and accomplishment. In the two leading roles, Anita Majumdar and Sanjay Talwar are, ethnicity notwithstanding, miscast. Talwar, a fine actor of gawks and geeks, makes the king's puzzled conscientiousness endearing sympathetic; but he is not a natural authority figure in a dramatic world that calls out for it. Majumdar, by contrast, is too worldly and controlled for Sakuntala's initial innocence. They both give us the outlines of their predicaments, but not the texture. The other players do a lot of doubling, some of it confusing. Indian audiences may know the story by heart; the rest of us need to have it told as well as decorated. It feels like a masterpiece, but we have to take a lot on trust. - Shakuntala runs until Feb. 15. Call 416-973-4000 for more information.

contact_edits.before: Kevin Hanchard matches her as a John with complementary hang-ups: sure of himself as a man, but still jumping shamefully to attention at the ring of the master's phone (a particularly effective update). He's cruel without being naturally callous; he has just as much compassion as he can afford. He's nettled and shamed not only by Julie but -- Strindberg's notorious misogyny being on hold in this play --by Raven Dauda's spirited and sensible Christine who, all dressed up in her Sunday-go-to-meeting, gives the play's religious imperatives an unaccustomed authority. She also, in an uncommonly handsome kitchen, attacks her chopping-block with an implacability that foreshadows the dispatching of Miss Julie's pet. Some of the scene setting is heavy-handed; John reads about Lyndon Johnson's signing of the Civil Rights Act and the murder of the freedom riders Goodman, Schwerner and Chaney in the same edition of the daily paper, dated the Fourth of July. And The Real Inspector Hound should have killed off the device by which, whenever someone turns on the radio, it's right at the start of either a song or a news bulletin. But most of the details fit beautifully into place. The brief shared dream of opening a jazz-club in Chicago--John as manager, Julie as hostess, Christine as cook-- rings true for all three of them; they must all have seen the same movies. The play Miss Julie is supposed to have the tension of an erotic nightmare. For once it does. - Miss Julie: Freedom Summer is at the Bluma Appel Theatre until March 7. For tickets and information call 416-368-3110

contact_edits.before: Jordan Pettle brings a welcome flamboyance and precision to Tzara (Jack to Henry's Algy) and David Storch's Joyce, though sometimes too muted, is fine in his prophetic utterances, as well as sporting a great cartoon outline. Oliver Dennis and Maggie Huculak are pitch perfect as the Lenins who, despite Stoppard's extensive rewrites, remain largely sealed off in their own part of the play, as in the sealed railway carriage that carried them back to Russia. Sarah Wilson and Krystin Pellerin are treats as the two young ladies, who end up butting heads and minds in a vaudeville duet ("oh, Gwendolen...oh, Cecilee") that might be even more pointed with more talking, less singing. contact_edits.before: Musical director Wayne Gwillim musters his forces impeccably; this is as well-sung a show as you'll find in Toronto. Remaining performers include Parris Greaves as a minister, Patricia Zentilli as a surprisingly soft-boiled agent and Allie Hughes, delightful as a waitress still smitten with childish adoration of Mr. Bungee, the frog-star employer who haunts Gordon's nightmares. He's played by Juan Chioran, who must be the tallest amphibian in captivity, and who seems happiest when he's allowed to take his head off and give Gordon a pep talk. His function seems to be to help our hero back to health by persuading him that writing cheerful songs for children can be a noble pursuit, as indeed it is. The really affecting journey in the show is a musician's one. Gordon's initial attempt to write a number called Frogs Have So Much Spring, in which neither he nor anyone else can believe, finally evolves into I Feel so Much Spring and, just before that, to the show's real climax Time and Music. Lindsay Anne Black designed the ingenious set; musical arrangements, carried over from the New York original, are by another fine composer (and finer lyricist), Jason Robert Brown. - A New Brain is at the Berkeley Street Theatre until Sunday. Call 416-368-3110 for tickets and information.

contact_edits.before: Pyaasa had more characters, more atmosphere and a bitterly ironic story. Letters to My Grandma is much slighter, more a two-headed lyric than a play. It does have an ear for detail, and Roy's acting, here as before, gets the best of two worlds: the formality of Eastern theatre and the naturalism of Western. She is very particular in delineating her roles, the grandmother's especially, while giving each a stark, stylized physical outline. She moves, and occasionally chants, with a grace that transcends prettiness. She executes thunderclap transformations from one role to the other, abetted by Thomas Morgan Jones' direction and, especially, David DeGrow's lighting. I don't know whether she's taken vows of theatrical solitude; personally, I'd like to see her follow Kristen Thomson's current example, and both act with and write for other performers. There's nothing aesthetically immoral about one-person shows, but a glut of them such as we are currently experiencing --mainly for economic reasons -- can leave an audience feeling starved. - Letters to my Grandma runs until March 8. Call 416-504-7529 for information.

contact_edits.before: The casting must be intended to provide a distancing effect, to avoid theobvious danger of self-exploitation. Up to a point it succeeds. Lucs, under Ashlie Corcoran's direction, makes no attempt to imitate Coleman, or indeed to do any kind of male impersonation at all. She's an actress with a strong physical and vocal presence that quite often goes into overdrive: I've never known so much juice to be squeezed from simple place-names. This wide-eyed over-emphasis, pervasive in the earlier parts of the evening, is the direct opposite of the discretion the play needs. It's the wrong kind of alienation. Later on, the performance settles down. A woman's body takes the curse off, while adding a comedic edge to, the narrator's rueful preoccupation with his own physicality. Lucs also of course gets to play all the women in the story, including Carole herself, whose spoken contributions are significantly minimal. That's a tactful decision on the author's part, and it communicates itself to the actress who becomes both simpler and more affecting as the play's emotions take hold. Naked autobiography in the theatre always seems to me like special pleading, sometimes amounting to emotional blackmail. This production, which I saw at a preview, can't avoid the first charge but keeps honourably clear of the second. - Tijuana Cure is at the Passe Muraille Backspace until March 28. Call 416-504-7529 for more information.

contact_edits.before: In fact, there is some Canadian content here. John Jarvis plays, deliriously well, a fellow who goes humorously mad and starts speaking with a Canadian accent. I'm not suggesting these conditions are coequal; his character is a traumatised war vet who starts channelling a slain Newfie comrade. He even talks of moving to Canada, though neither he nor the play gets far in this direction. He also has apocalyptic visions in which he foresees the atomic bomb, the oil race and Monty Python. Others delightful are Paul Braunstein as a dogged but not quite dashing seducer, and as the oracular aunt, the still-youngish Michelle Fisk taking subtle advantage of age's privilege to stay comparatively still and quiet. Julie Stewart puts on a bold comic face as a semi-willing adulteress (the spirit is willing, etc.) and John Cleland blusters effectively as the bathroom magnate. Of the two putative heroines, Lisa Norton has an intriguingly baleful air as Martha the reluctant, not to say incompetent, maid; Kerry Ann Doherty smiles prettily as Jane, but the character's a hole in the play. As a text, And Up They Flew is earthbound, but the production flaps wings. - And Up They Flew runs until April 4 at the Berkeley Street Theatre Upstairs. For tickets, call 416-368-3110 or visit theatrecolumbus.ca.

contact_edits.before: Twin performances that make the Mamet pauses sing come from Peter Donaldson as the most abrasive member of the sales force, nursing grudges from way back, and William Webster, jowly and pouchy, as the most pathetic, facing the same defeat as Levene but without the same fight in him. Jordan Pettle gets the manager absolutely right, savouring his power and, beneath his collegiate veneer, as ruthless and venal a barracuda as the boys out in the field. Ken MacDonald's sets do well by the restaurant, less well by the office; the two are symbolically linked when the wall menu of one turns into the contest-scoreboard of the other. I'm not convinced that a play at once so full and so spare needs this kind of illustration, but I guess it serves for a play in which dog voraciously eats dog after first sharing a table with him. - Glengarry Glen Ross runs until May 9. Call 416-866-8666 for tickets.

contact_edits.before: Back in Toronto, I recommend Fear of Flight, though more for its presentation than its substance. Originating (quite some time ago) with the Artistic Fraud company of Newfoundland, this depicts a storm-tossed cross-country plane trip, with vignettes of the passengers' past lives supplied by playwrights from all points along the flight path. Only one of these (written by Daniel MacIvor, performed by Mia Mansfield as an innocent lady travelling at the behest of Jesus, who in this incarnation sounds like a con man) is especially enlivening, but it's the group effort that counts. While hanging firmly on to their individual identities, the 14 actors combine brilliantly in a kind of acted ballet to which they also provide non-stop a cappella accompaniment. Jillian Keiley's production justifies the mountainous regard in which she's held across Canada. Actually, she'd already done that, for me, with her magnificent staging of Creon, the penultimate play in Ned Dickens's City of Wine cycle. The ultimate one, too--Seven, directed by Sarah Garton Stanley -- was a fine piece of vocal and visual orchestration, with the highest overall standard of acting (by mature York students) of the entire enterprise. Both plays brought the chorus to the forefront of the action: brilliantly so in Creon, which brought the Antigone story to new life, with too much repetition but to ultimately stirring effect in Seven. Collecting these last two episodes confirmed some of my earlier preconceptions, overturned others. Somebody remount the whole thing so I can write about it again. - Brief Encounters is in repertory through Oct. 24 at the Festival Theatre, Niagara-on-the-Lake. Call 1-800-511-SHAW for tickets. Fear of Flight runs through May 24 at the Factory Theatre. Call 416-504-9971 for details.

contact_edits.before: The two girls match them, with Sara Topham's impregnable hauteur as Gwendolen balanced by Andrea Runge's demurer steeliness as Cecily. As Reverend Chasuble, Stephen Ouimette, a visual symphony of limbs and gaiters, wafts phantasmally through the manor-house garden; Sarah Dodd's Miss Prism melts delightfully though always respectably in his presence. I thought at first she overdid her suburban asperity towards Cecily, on whom she is after all dependent, but on reflection she makes an excellent point. Prism, though personally as blinkered as Lady Bracknell, is the play's social conscience, prevented as a governess from aping the aristocracy as the butlers and valets do. And she has her unwitting revenge. One wouldn't want to throw the baby out with the bath-water, but leaving it in a handbag is an outrage as revolutionary as Aunt Augusta knew in her threatened bones that it would be. - The Importance of Being Earnest is in repertory through Oct. 30. 1-800-567-1600.

contact_edits.before: There's satisfying work from Jonathan Goad as a gambling gallant who loses one heiress and gets another, older but richer (note that, in a comedy without a love story, he's the closest thing to a hero); from Randy Hughson and Victor Ertmanis as a pair of pimps who put a couple of respectable women on the game, right under their husbands' noses; from Jesse Aaron Dwyer as a conscientious cutpurse; Michael Spencer-Davis in the minute role of an officer; and Cliff Saunders who runs a great puppet-show. The show itself is a production highlight, and though some of the fairground jollity is run-of-the-mill, there is also some good surprise staging and an unusually intelligent placing of actors in the auditorium. Jonsonian comedy, combining a thick text with the action of a farce, is a tough act; this is an encouraging start at cracking it. - Bartholomew Fair is in repertory through Oct. 2. Call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.cafor tickets and information.

He's a boy (Kolton Stewart, a touching Macduff Junior in Macbeth) who wanders on at the beginning, the end and halfway through, as some kind of symbol of lost innocence and/or future hope. He gets to sing Somewhere, a song that reinforces its lyricist's contention that it should have stayed an instrumental. The show isn't already sentimental enough? contact_edits.before: However, the fine individual performances don't cohere into relationships; the actors keep having to jump guns. Some cuts get in their way; so do some awkward choices. The veiled antagonism, brilliantly taut in the text, between the too-confident Antony and the coming man Octavius (one of the great small roles) is muffed. The crowd that becomes a mob isn't believable in either mood or from any period, for the forum orations they're placed among us, ad-libbing in our ears but with their real, crucial reactions out of focus. There's a new character billed as Soothsayer's Girlfriend, rather a specialized job description and one she doesn't seem to take very seriously since she's away from her partner, a cripple in a go-cart, in his scene of greatest need. More importantly, his lowly position means that when he gives Caesar his straight-up tip about the ides of March, the two can't make eye contact. So another key moment goes. The play remains locked behind its picture frame. Very flat, the Avon. - Julius Caesar is in repertory until Oct. 31. Call 1-800-567- 1600 or visit stratfordfestival.cafor more information.

contact_edits.before: Derek Boyes seems whimsically out of place as her perennially defeated husband, substituting a Celtic smile for a Yiddish shrug. William Webster might profitably be more whimsical as Jacob, who retreats by playing Caruso records, but he does the secular-prophet bit imposingly well. A shame that he has to make his greatest contribution to the plot from offstage. Michael Hanrahan, with a silk scarf wrapped around his vocal chords, is absolutely right as the familys comparatively rich Uncle Morty, and Ari Cohen righter than right as Moe whose amputation on the last day of the war made him a cynic, a pacifist and--as it transpires -- an unlikely do-gooder. The young people are very impressive: Jonathan Gould quivering with life as the irresolute Ralph, Sarah Wilson hard as nails as Hennie and Matthew Edison is lovely as the poor schmuck tricked into giving Hennie's child a father. It would be hard, and probably wrong, to play the last life-affirming moments for irony. But taken straight they seem wished for, tacked-on. Play and production are awake, no question, but they don't sing. - Awake and Sing! runs through July 31 at the Young Centre for the Performing Arts. Visit youngcentre.cafor details. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

contact_edits.before: Ever Yours, Oscar has been devised by Peter Wylde; Bedford directs himself. It doesn't pretend to be a play, and it's fragmentary even as a recital. Bedford reads or speaks at a music stand, placed about three quarters of the way upstage (anyone sitting behind in this three-handed space will have only his back to look at) with a large portrait of Wilde hanging on the back wall. In between epistles, he delivers snippets of basic biography. The Sturm und Drang of Wilde's life are given bare-bones treatment; we hear very little of, or to, Bosie, though what we do hear makes him sound more appalling than ever. There's nothing from the anguished De Profundis, technically a letter but hardly an informal one. Basically, the show gives us sidelights, mainly delightful ones; ranging from the young Oscar admonishing his mother on what to send him at prep school to the enfant terrible Oscar on his lecture tour of the United States, instructing silver miners on the subject of modern art. (They hated the art, loved the artist -- i. e. him.) In short --and it is short -- this is not a momentous evening or, preferably, afternoon. But it offers insights, and one of our very finest actors being very fine. - Ever Yours, Oscar is in repertory through Aug. 29. Visit stratfordfestival.ca or call 1-800-567-1600 for tickets and information.

contact_edits.before: Neither the play nor its author are dismissible; Orton, unlike the self-satisfied rebels of London's Royal Court, was a real subversive, a working-class gay man who'd done time and ended up being bludgeoned to death by his lover. He had a genuine outsider's vision, one most completely and resourcefully expressed in his next and last play What the Butler Saw. Loot works perfectly on its own terms, but they're narrow terms. One personal complaint. When Truscott discovers Mrs. McLeavy's preserved corpse he asks, "whose mummy is this?" to which Hal replies, truthfully but without thinking, "mine." I always thought that was the funniest line in the play. It isn't here; the timing is off. But that doesn't happen often. - Loot is in repertory at the Young Centre through Aug. 1. Call 416-866-8666 for tickets and information.

contact_edits.before: Hughson and Ouimette get their laughs cleanly on the lines. Bruce Dow, in the star role of Pseudolus, acts fussily around his; he only comes into focus when he duets with Ouimette on the reprise of Lovely, the comic love-duet (already a hoot when the young 'uns do it). Most spectacularly miscalculated is Dan Chameroy's Miles Gloriosus ( "braggart soldier") who should be impregnably self-satisfied and terrifying, but is here made of jelly. But the actor hardly stands a chance in a production that has a single chariot wheel careening across the stage before his entrance, thus undercutting his immortal first line, "Stand aside, everyone! I take large steps!" Lycus is an underwritten role but Cliff Saunders' decision to play him as an epicene eccentric rather than a mercenary man of business is not a happy one. His non-speaking merchandise includes regular Stratford adornment Sara Topham, who may not be playing Medea later this week, as the song says, but was once a memorable Cassandra, and is obviously having a ball here. They've cut Pretty Little Picture, which is unforgivable, but they're not the first. The show remains irresistible. It all turns out all right. It has to. - A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum is in repertory through Nov. 1. Call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.cafor tickets and information.

contact_edits.before: This doesn't affect the clown scenes, which are unusually good, with Mark Crawford's Trinculo dignified as well as craven and Jason Gray's Stephano growing in self-importance by the moment. They're a very believable pair of drunks, while Caliban and Trinculo, sharing a cloak, make a great pantomime horse. The cutting of the first scene makes the courtiers' roles seem thinner than ever, but the actors fight back with Robert Dodds' king as credibly conscious-stricken as any I've seen. There's some gender-alteration here, too, and it works well with Liz Gordon's Gonzala. The supposed ace, though, is that Prospera's usurping sibling is also a woman: a juicy idea, except that the two never meet till the last scene, during which the evil Antonia is almost silent. The sisters are reduced to throwing glances at one another, and in fact Tracy Ferencz's Antonia does project a powerful image of unredemption. In the earlier scene in which she tempts Sebastian (Karl Ang) to regicide, the production underplays its hand; the two are shown as already being lovers, though it would be more effective to have the sexual and political seductions play out simultaneously. Economics mean that most of the spirits' masque has to go, but that's hardly a loss; what magic we do see is inventive. This is a lightweight production but it isn't dumb. It's the best Dream anyone has had in High Park in years. - The Tempest runs through Sept. 6 at the Dream in High Park. Call 416-368-3110 for details.

contact_edits.before: Another show with some songs (old-fashioned but nice) is The Menaechmus Twins, one of whose characters, a Roman slave, at one point makes as if about to sing about being free but then stops himself, as if he doesn't want to go into competition with Stephen Sondheim. This makes sense, as this play is by Plautus, whose ancient Roman comedies inspired A Funny Thing Happened on the Way to the Forum, though it's one that Forum didn't use. It did, though, inspire Shakespeare, whose Comedy of Errors added some sentiment and an extra pair of lookalikes. You may wonder if he really improved it much, since this open-air production is a total delight in its own right. Plautus at least explains why his long-separated twins should have the same first name, which is more than Shakespeare did. He also provided a tidier expository prologue, which the uncredited translation (in which someone "fills a fine freighter full of ... freight") gleefully exploits; as does Melee Hutton's production, brazenly presenting us with supposedly identical twins who are, at most, of about the same height. Wayne Ward gives a wonderfully self-satisfied account of the dark-haired married one, who finds himself excluded ( "I'm the most shuttest-out man alive") by wife and mistress, both of them played, as in some Freudian nightmare and deliciously, by the same actress, Sarah Evans. His fair-haired bachelor sibling is Ryan Hollyman, who plays on one flustered note but holds it well. Adrian Proszowski as one brother's servant and Jeffrey R. Smith as the other's parasite are towers of supporting strength. There is a basic two-door set, neatly used, and no need of lighting, since the show starts at 6 p. m. and is over at 7:20. It's early, short, hilarious and you pay what you can. The best theatrical deal in town. - The Harder They Come runs through Aug. 23 at the Canon Theatre. Call 416-872-1212 for ticket and schedule details. The Menaechmus Twins runs in Withrow Park through Aug. 9. Visit theatreworksproductions.comfor more information.

Gray also does his share of expert mimicry, both as singer and composer; there's one song in which he sounds, whether by accident or design, like a dead vocal ringer for Randy Newman. Peterson himself remains a sharp-eyed scamp underneath it all, a jewel in a cock-eyed Canadian crown. contact_edits.before: Dion Johnstone's Oberon struts and poses like Michael Jackson; now, was this the production's starting point or a topical addition? Yanna Mc-Intosh's Titania is compelling in sections, among them the lament for her friend who died "of being mortal" and her bulletin on climate change, which for once gets reflected in the staging; there's snow this midsummer night. Tom Rooney's Puck casts an even more potent spell when he warns about the lost souls of ghostly suicides; elsewhere, an original performance seems trapped within its pop carapace. As for the mortal monarchs: Timothy D. Stickney is an urbane Theseus, but the production goes for the fashionable idea about Hippolyta being reluctant to marry him. This means as usual that the actress has to tie herself in knots trying to inject hostility into a speech that's plainly a celebration, and then has to stand around miming a mental journey that never gets mentioned in the text. The production then perversely underplays the couple's really important conflict: their differing views on imagination, which is only what the play's about. Still, the final coming together of all the different worlds is beautifully done, justifying a finale ultimo in which the entire cast breaks into wild celebratory dance. With effects like that, the show is a crowd-pleaser. But it's pleasing on deeper levels as well. - A Midsummer Night's Dream is in repertory through Oct. 30. Call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.cafor tickets and information.

I have a favourite theory about the Four Seasons' establishing hits, Sherry and the even better Big Girls Don't Cry, which is that with the extreme and abrupt contrasts between their high highs and low lows, they're funny. Well, that's how they sounded to my generation in London, where we couldn't have cared whether they came from New Jersey or New York or New Orleans. I tried my theory out on Gaudio, but he wasn't having it. Well, he did admit that "some of our songs have been quite humorous," and he did admit that the bass voice owed something to the cartoon sound of Yogi Bear, who at the time was even more popular than Sherry. But, he says, "we don't allow parodies of any kind. We wouldn't want to make light of songs that have moved people." And, obviously, are moving them still. - Jersey Boys is onstage now at the Toronto Centre for the Arts. For tickets and show-times, visit dancaptickets.comor call 416-644-3665.

contact_edits.before: Zastrozzi, directed by Jennifer Tarver, is the best time I've ever had at a George F. Walker play, dislodging Panych's Shaw Festival production of Nothing Sacred. Both these works, jokey literary extravaganzas in half-imaginary landscapes, sidestep the credibility problems that afflict Walker's plays set inpresentday Toronto. Zastrozzi is a jaundiced 20th-century lampoon of the romantic 19th-century vision of sanguinary 17th-century Italy: a Revenger's Comedy in which philosophy rules, and kills. Tarver's production impresses from its first moment: a monologue, scared and scary for Oliver Becker as a befuddled Renaissance thug who looks and sounds like Tony Soprano in reduced circumstances. Zastrozzi, "master of discipline," is the ultimate practical critic, pursuing a homicidal vendetta against bad artists; in Rick Roberts's performance, he's a sinner as impregnable as any saint. His particular prey, brilliantly twittered by Andrew Shaver, is Verezzi, a weak-minded painter who also stands accused of killing Zastrozzi's mother. How and why are never quite revealed; and strangely, when the two antagonists come finally face to face (over a heap of corpses), the matter is never mentioned. The play goes down a lot of blind alleys, narrative and intellectual. You can't, in the end, take it seriously; but you can relish it as a young man's high-style high-wire act. The best performance of all, and much his best at Stratford, is John Vickery's as Verezzi's unshakably conscientious guardian, a cropped black wig surmounting a face that's a white mask of determination and despair. - The Trespassers is in repertory through Oct. 4; Rice Boy and Zastrozzi through Oct. 3. Call 1-800-567-1600 or visit stratfordfestival.cafor tickets and information.

contact_edits.before: There's a third leading character who's said to be a critic by trade but spends his time hanging out with the stars and receiving their confidences; the job has certainly gone downhill in the last century or so. Diego Matamoros' role is similar to the one he had in The Play's the Thing, but this one's been removed from the controlling centre to the suffering sidelines. Anyway, in an evening where metatheatrics are already running riot, it's a pleasure to watch another instalment in the long-running, and constantly shifting, Schultz-Matamoros double act; no two actors play better together. A good supporting cast includes Dawn Greenhalgh as Ilona's dresser turned surrogate-mother (and Nandor's newly acquired and fearsome mother-in-law); Michael Simpson as an obsequious debt-collector who can be bought off with complimentary tickets; and Jennifer Phipps as an usherette who conveys, mostly in silence, that she knows exactly what she's worth and won't take a pfennig less. Camellia Koo's sets and Judith Bowden's costumes redeem the reputation of chocolate-box design: apt for a play with a sweet surface and a hard centre. - The Guardsman is in repertory at the Young Centre through Oct. 24. contact_edits.before: The play juxtaposes, and exposes, two barren marriages. While George and Martha delight in stripping their marital scars in company, Nick and Honey have theirs dragged, cajoled or threatened out of them -- and they're at least equally grievous. As Nick, envied and mocked by George as the wave of the scientific future, Tim Campbell is perfect: broad-shouldered, self-satisfied, his limited sympathies subsiding as his insecurities increase. The recurring description of Diana Donnelly's Honey as "slim-hipped" here seems like just another of the characters' games but she beautifully registers the trophy bride's progress from delicious shock to shock absolute. Fine as all four performances are individually, the real prize of Diana Leblanc's production is the phenomenal degree of contact between them. There is never a moment at which either action or reaction goes slack, and both the pacing and the placing are impeccable. Astrid Janson's gaunt, precipitous set is a suitably gladiatorial arena, with a couple of oddities. The books are mostly painted, suggesting that even the household's literacy is suspect, and the shelves are adorned with pictures of George and Martha's namesakes, the Washingtons: Is this the production getting cute or are the characters? I still have doubts as to whether the play signifies much beyond its very enjoyable self. But that self is substantial: dialogue that stings, action that builds, characters who've become archetypes and -- it now appears -- compassion. In its 11 years, Soulpepper has given us any number of good productions and a handful of great ones. This is one of the greats. - Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf ? is in repertory through Oct. 24 at the Young Centre. For tickets and information visit soulpepper.caor call 416-866-8666. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

contact_edits.before: After all of which, it's awkward to have to admit that the show is always involving and ultimately moving. Credit goes to the history, to the music and to the fact that the creators, however much they fumble, do seem genuinely involved with the subject. The cast helps, too: Richard Harte, Brandon McGibbon, Tracy Dawson and Jacquelyn French give pungent if oddly uneasy accounts of team players and team fans, while Richard McMillan as priestly team coach takes some stock jokes and good intentions and makes a man of them. But it's John and Mary who really lump our throats by letting us partake in their growing up. Tony LePage is lithe, sympathetic and, when bitterness is called for, powerful. Peck is superb, confirming what she promised in We Will Rock You: that she's a first-rate theatre singer who's also a charming and economical actress, forceful without forcing and capable of projecting a passionate moral strength. It's a strangely admirable show. Let me put it like this: It's often dumb, but it's not stupid. - The Boys in the Photograph is at the Royal Alexandra Theatre until Nov. 1. For tickets and information call 416-872-1212 or visit mirvish.com.

contact_edits.before: There's humour, though less than the show or its first-night audience might like to think. Anna D. Shapiros production seems to have coarsened on the road, and to be aimed at people who think it shockingly funny to hear mature actresses using four-letter words. Most of the cast give in at some time or other; even Shannon Cochran, who otherwise dispenses a fastidious brand of swaggering self-hatred as Barbara, goes for an easy laugh at the second-act curtain. (She gets it; the public appetite for bad acting seems inexhaustible.) There's one character I haven't mentioned: a Cheyenne housekeeper (DeLanna Studi) who spends the first scene giving comfort to Beverly, the last giving it to Violet, and in between proves a very good cook and a great defender of virtue. Even the toughest American plays can wind up sentimental, and the final curtain of this one finds Violet the hitherto-untouchable curled up in the lap of the Indian (her word, though the others try to persuade her it's "Native American"). Perhaps this is a metaphor for America. Or it could just be a gimmick. - August: Osage County runs until Nov. 15. contact_edits.before: Four actors share the other roles, all of them with guns blazing. Christopher Hunt is the most extrovert of all as, ironically, the crybaby shrink, constantly ducking beneath his lintel. Rebecca Northan is invigoratingly sharp and smart; Damien Atkins dazzles in three roles, two of them unlike any I have seen him play before. Melody A. Johnson pushes a bit too hard in her earlier incarnations; attack is not her natural mode. But she makes up for it a millionfold as the centenarian, first glimpsed bobbing enchantingly around in the recesses of her room, then emerging for an enchanting duet with Anderson that she plays with unnervingly calm assurance and with timing of almost unholy perfection. This is a very funny play, even by Panych's standards, but this scene had me literally breathless with delight. Johnson has a speech about the Louvre that's a miracle. - 7 Stories continues to Dec. 5. Call 416-368-3110 for ticket information.

contact_edits.before: Probably, given enough time, any three people could torment each other as effectively, but the devils at the end of the phone seem to want quick results. It does mean though that, dramatically speaking, there is something arbitrary about the whole set-up, reinforced by Sartre's inability to bring his dead characters to life. There's nothing especially compelling about their earthly biographies, or about how they're revealed to us, and the ways in which they torture one another are surprisingly limited. But if the play can't develop its conception, except to a pre-ordained philosophic conclusion, the conception itself is genius. And it's in illustrating it, drilling into it, that Collier's production is at its strongest. We are watching the actors, most of the time, in giant unforgiving close-up, and they respond with performances that are ingrained and unflinching. Andy Thompson's vulpine Cradeau tends to generalize, but the women are fiercely specific, Laara Sadiq's bruised incisiveness as Inez balancing the elegant meltdown of Lucia Frangione's Estelle. The triple screen isolates them, and accentuates the moments when one crosses into another's territory. Just occasionally an aerial surveillance shot shows us the whole room, an oppressively ornate Second Empire chamber, with heavy ornaments that can't be lifted and a door that mostly won't open (and when it does, doesn't lead anywhere you'd dare to go). Hell is also other furniture; and the sight of the three of them marooned there is far more powerful than in the sustained long-shot of a conventional staging. See them in hell. - No Exit closes tonight at Buddies in Bad Times Theatre. For ticket information, call 416-955-0101.

contact_edits.before: The style's side effects include recurrent outbreaks of whiny or rhetorical acting. In Eda Holmes' production, only two actors are immune. One is Juan Chioran, who as the painter is required to speak Italian and to sing, both of which he does with great melodiousness, but who is equally cool and commanding when talking in English. The other, in a tougher part and with less experience to draw on, is Marc Bendavid whose troubled, passionate naivete as the priest is the evening's driving force, He doesn't bring off the end when, having suffered a dire transformation, he has to persuade us that something has actually happened, but I doubt if anyone could. The normally luminous Jenny Young is bafflingly uneven as Mary of the Secrets, sometimes in command, sometimes just shouting. As the physician, Brian Dooley hardly gets beyond gruff rudeness, though I think he's meant to be a cynical teller of unwelcome truths. Nicola Correia-Damude begins arrestingly as Mary of the Sheets, but then finds nowhere to go; ditto Miranda Edwards' Mary Frances who gets very sulky. As the deluded Mary Anne, a key role judging from her position in the curtain call, Shannon Taylor has some piercing moments but mostly picks her way through her words as if they were a minefield. If I haven't engaged with the play's deeper themes (faith, art, etc.) that's because I can't detect where they are. And to be honest, I don't care. - The Madonna Painter runs until Dec. 13. Call 416-504-4060 or visit factorytheatre.cafor tickets and information. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

contact_edits.before: The original play starts with the police threatening to break the heads of protesters and ends with a description of what sounds like kettling. Its main concerns are an intractable economic crisis and the thwarting of reform by special interests. It all seems, when you read it, blazingly topical. It has some of the same effect onstage but not as much, because the action, what there is of it, doesn't so much carry the ideas as buckle under them. That's true of both versions, though on consideration I prefer the original, ugly warts and all. The rewrite gives the final moment to Chavenders secretary. It doesn't mean much because, even though she's played by Mary Haney, we don't know anything about her. ? On the Rocks runs until Oct. 8. For tickets, call 1-800-511-7429 or visit shawfest.com.

contact_edits.before: The most piercing speech of all, as it was in the original, is that of the young Trinidadian girl who was overjoyed to be brought to Canada to join her mother, and who then found herself being abused by her stepfather. I never expected to find a performance in this role that rivalled that of dbi.young, but Thais Francis is equally moving, both in her initial joy and in her later shame and terror. Unfortunately she's subjected, like everyone in the cast only more so, to amplification that makes her sound as if her voice were coming from some place else. Presumably the face mics are there for the musical sections, but it's shameful to keep them on for the dialogue; the Enwave is not exactly a big theatre. It adds to the feeling that the songs and dances aren't earning their keep. (There's already a musical about hair, and several about kinks.) Giving each character both a speech and a song makes the show feel repetitive; this, on top of the pacing problems already noted, makes it feel long. ? da Kink in My Hair runs through Aug. 21 at the Enwave Theatre, Harbourfront. Call 416-973-4000 or visit tickets.harbourfrontcentre.com for ticket information.

contact_edits.before: At the opposite extreme: The most visually and conceptually exciting theatre in Toronto has been happening, not for the first time, at the Canadian Opera Company. Its production of Gluck's Iphigenia in Tauris, in its compression and concentration, cut to the merciless heart of concentration and compression. Its Rigoletto was set in a plush 19thcentury men's club, brilliantly created by the great Canadian designer Michael Levine. The program notes claimed that this was a comment on the patriarchal society in which the story is set, but it was selling itself short; what we saw was a privileged group ganging up on all outsiders, including the crippled clowning protagonist; which is what the Verdi work is all about. (The singing in both productions was great, too, but you expect that.) ? Circumcise Me runs through Nov. 6 at the Jane Mallett Theatre. For showtimes and ticket information visit hgjewishtheatre.com or call 416-366-7723.

contact_edits.before: There's some confusion in the musical theatre and opera divisions: sometimes they overlap, sometimes they don't. Let me just note that best musical actor nominees include critical winners Bruce dow and darrin Baker (leading and supporting respectively, for us); that I wish some space could have been found for Christopher Siebert in La Cage Aux Folles, even if he was just passing through; and that I was glad to see Falsettos (musical) and Dialogue Aux Carmelites (opera) nominated for best production in their respective categories, though I was sad to see no mention of their respective directors, robert McQueen and robert Carsen. In the latter case, I'm more than sad; I'm incensed. Dialogue aux Carmelies was the COC's finest production of a fine season, maybe their finest production in years. It may also have been the best thing seen last season on any Toronto stage. robert.cushman@hotmail.com The Dora Awards are at the Bluma Appel Theatre on Monday June 24.

contact_edits.before: He has fewer regrets than when we last met him, but those he has are choice. Like Manon, though less consistently, he's obsessed with the image of the play's third title character, which becomes gradually more visible as John van Burek's production proceeds. (Van Burek is directing his own excellent translation). Thoughts of the Madonna are what bring Manon and Sandra thematically together: that and some childhood reminiscences. A feeling of regret, of something missed, hangs in the air at the end, but it isn't as compelling as the monologues, respectively shaming and shameless. contact_edits.before: The nightclub of their encounter occasions the best-staged, bestdanced and (by Charlotte Dean) best-costumed number of the evening, "Rich Man's Frug." Second best is Charity's triumphant "I'm a Brass Band," with her applauding chorus costumed not as bandsmen but as commuters; the actual steps are nothing special but the concept connects most satisfyingly with that of the production as a whole. Other bits of Parker Esse's choreography seem messy or hemmed-in. Martell's dancing, in a role created for Gwen Verdon, is less than her acting and singing; when she teams up with her two best buddies and confidantes for "There's Gotta Be Something Better Than This," it's hard not to agree with the song-title, while "If My Friends Could See Me Now," her hat-and-cane specialty, never takes off. But her personality carries her through, all the way to a conclusion that Panych has staged with exemplary tact. The original production ended with a gag; the movie (Fosse's, not Fellini's) ended with syrup. This one goes for honesty, expressed in a lovely closing image of wistful defiance. All along, Charity has been asking for respect. She finally gets it. National Post robert.cushman@hotmail.com

contact_edits.before: Act Two features a band of semicannibals whose vocabulary derives entirely from Italian cuisine; and what passes for humour depends entirely on stepping cutely out of context. The only ingenuity comes in the way the story finally dovetails with J. M. Barrie's original; the only emotion piggybacks shamelessly on that same source. In these respects it's like Wicked, but probably worse. Charlie Gallant makes a good impression as Peter. Kate Besworth is the Wendyish young lady who rescues and inspires him; it's a repeat of her performance in Arcadia, which I've certainly no objection to seeing again. The boy discovers leadership but the girl is always ahead of him; we get it already. So did Barrie. Martin Happer is the future Captain Hook, prone to accidents and anachronisms; he gives it a good shot but Ross Petty would do it more natural. A large cast pitches enthusiastically in; Jackie Maxwell's production relies heavily on standardized methods of suggesting waves and storms, and on the supposed outrageousness of Shaw Festival actors dressing up like mermaids (them again) for a musical number. The Broadway reviews made the play sound interesting: fooled again. A plague on all prequels, say I. robert.cushman@hotmail.com

contact_edits.before: Canadian Stage/York University directing program), Mrozeski is amazingly sensitive to text, a quality that might pay even bigger dividends in a more sympathetic acoustic. He lets us get inside the characters' heads. The play's setup is simple, though brilliantly spun out; two pairs of long-separated identical twins - one resident in Ephesus, the other visiting - are regularly mistaken for one another, so that they come to believe that all around them are mad and are thought to be mad themselves. The visiting couple (Dylan Trowbridge as Antipholus of Syracuse, Naomi Wright as his servant Dromio) have the richer opportunities for bemusement, and take them; for maybe the first time I found myself not only laughing at their predicament but sympathizing with it; this must be how it feels to be gradually convinced that you're surrounded by sorcerers. Moving through and behind the farce is a thread of incipient tragedy; Aegeon, father of the twin Antipholi, is under sentence of death as an illegal alien, and is saved only when recognition leads to reprieve. Allan Louis, again, makes his opening expository monologue compelling and his penultimate despair very moving (though he really should speak up a bit). So the joy at the close really hits home. It's common knowledge that the family reunions in Shakespeare's last plays can move you to tears. It now appears that this, one of his first, can work the same magic robert.cushman@hotmail.com

contact_edits.before: CRITIC'S PICKTHEATREThree winners: There is everything to celebrate about A Whistle in the Dark (Berkeley Street Upstairs; 416-368-3110), but the greatest thrill is to see Joseph Ziegler, playing the paterfamilias of a brawling brood, turn before your eyes from an excellent actor to a great one. As he stands on a chair at the play's terrible climax, he sums up a whole complex character, a pitiable blusterer with a poetic streak who has raised evasion to an art form. This Anglo-Irish play, 44 years old and worth the wait, is an early work by the veteran Tom Murphy. The direction, by visiting Hibernian Jason Byrne, and the other seven performances are only perfect. The Bear (The Grange Room at AGO; 416-979-6608) is an adventurous site- specific production of a Chekhov farce, hilarious and also subtle, with David Ferry at top speed, finding the nuances in a more sympathetic blowhard.
